en: Private Notes on the Essential Meanings of the Wording and Phrases of the Sublime Sūtra, Volume One:
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyún of Shígǔ Monastery.
Essential Meaning of the Second Chapter, "Expedient Means."
This sutra opens the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*) and reveals the mark of reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*). As the sutra states: "After a long time, the Buddhas must surely speak the truth.
Since it is the truth, why is the title of the first chapter called the "Chapter on Skillful Means" (*Upāya-parivarta*)?

Some ancient commentators explain this by saying it is named after the past; since the past is designated as "skillful means," the present is thereby understood to have the meaning of "reality. However, this... [is not so].
This is clear.
To claim that the name "expedient means" (upāya) is not found anywhere while asserting that there is no such textual statement, and that the meaning is also untenable, is incorrect.

Furthermore, since the intent of the sutra is precisely to establish this name in order to offer praise, to interpret it in such a way as to disparage it would surely be a repudiation of the text. How could this be?
I have never heard of anything so utterly contrary to the letter while deviating from the meaning. What I have heard differs from this [interpretation];

it is precisely the skillful means (*upāya*) of this sutra, which is what is called "wondrous. When the text asks, "For what reason does he so earnestly praise the foremost skillful means of all Buddhas?"—this is its very meaning.
This does not conflict with the letter or meaning of other sutras or the treatises of this sutra.

"However, why not simply proclaim 'the true reality' (*tattva*) directly, rather than distinguishing it separately so as to avoid confusion? Must one necessarily follow this general approach to eliminate all errors?

It is said: "There is a reason for this. It is because [the term 'true reality'] serves to establish the substantial entity (*vastu*) common to both self and others, and because these two capacities are thereby manifested.
If one were to speak merely of 'true reality,' these two meanings would be lost; therefore, it is not permissible. This is truly because this person’s name is universally known."

That all current texts follow these three distinct interpretations of the current text is indeed for a specific reason. The first follows the general [meaning], the second follows both the general and the specific, and the last follows only the specific.
People themselves are deluded; it is not that the title is redundant, for they are simply confused by the term "miao" (wondrous).
If this were so, a single sentence would suffice; why then are there four? The answer is that the principles and meanings require it.
This is because that meaning is fully contained within the sūtra. Since all four [alternatives] are present, why is the answer given by way of a single heading?
It is because one wishes to exhaustively discuss the principles of all dharmas; thus, the four alternatives are required to clarify the meaning of perfect subtlety.

Since the four are identical to the one, and the one is complete with the four, it is titled by means of the one. If that is so, any [number of alternatives] would suffice—why necessarily four? [Response: Toward... (the preceding question).

Having briefly clarified this, it shall now be explained further: because the beginning is cited to include the end; because the root is cited to encompass the branches; because one’s own cultivation is taught so as to cause others to attain the same;

and because the Dharma-realm is manifested in its entirety as a single great dependent origination, where principle is fully expressed through phenomena and essence is fully expressed through function.
If this is so, why does the commentary still rely on the third [category]—relying on the text for the words and relying on the meaning for the interpretation?

Because [the preceding] was brief, the Buddha himself praised both "expediency" (*upāya*) and "wonderful" (*adbhuta*). This single phrase is explained as being equivalent to the four phrases; for what reason, then, are ten pairs further clarified?
The meaning of "expediency" encompasses the horizontal and vertical, as well as cultivation and nature, self and other;

these are all fully present in the texts and meanings of the sutras. The four phrases explained above pertain only to the horizontal meaning, whereas cultivation and nature, self and... [the vertical].

Since the establishment of the meaning (*artha-vyavasthāpana*) has not yet been fully revealed, it is now that the ten pairs manifest its underlying intent. Why must it be explained by means of eight gates?

It is because the intended meaning of this sutra must necessarily proceed in this manner before its full force and scope can be exhausted; moreover, such is indeed the nature of these skillful means (*upāya*).
If that were so, one might object that four meanings should be complete here, yet there is no further need for them, nor is there any contemplative understanding (*vipaśyanā-bodha*).
Why is this so? This indeed possesses a profound significance. Since the former sages did not explain it and later worthies have likewise failed to clarify it, even I am unable to know it now.
"The younger generation is to be feared"—surely there will be capable individuals in the future.

Furthermore, some of the intermediate ranks may say that because the fourfold contemplation (*catuskoṭi*) is a common discourse within our school, it has been omitted here; however, I maintain that this is not the case.

These three meanings are also frequently discussed; since they are now present here, one might fear that it is not appropriate for the contemplation gate (*kanmon*) alone to be considered the most essential among them.
Now, let me attempt to explain this: the interpretation of the four-line contemplation (*shiku kan*) presented later is entirely identical to what follows, as will be self-evident;
therefore, I shall omit it here. Furthermore, there are other underlying intentions which you should naturally comprehend later on, though these are merely provisional means (*hōben*).
The meaning of this connection is as follows: if you wish to hear its essential points, may it be possible? Yet this is not easy; let me attempt to speak of it.
Because one is able to attain the wondrous reality for oneself and others, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*); "reality" (*tattva*) is the essence of principle (*li-ti*).
It is also called the Mahāyāna *pratītyasamutpāda*. In the following passage concerning the "great cause and condition," this clarifies its application for the sake of the multitudes.
Birth constitutes the dependent origination of the cause and effect of the One Vehicle.

If it is said that "the Buddha-seed arises from conditions," this is also spoken of in terms of its functional application as the dependent origination for sentient beings to cultivate and manifest their nature.

Furthermore, the subsequent passage states, "constantly acting as the causal condition for the Mahāyāna"; this too refers to its functional application. In sum, these three passages all concern the reality of the essence itself.

By manifesting wondrous functions to enable others to attain this One Vehicle (Ekayāna) through causes and conditions as a skillful means, one knows that the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṛiccheda*) of the present sutra is the causal condition for both oneself and others to attain the sublime Dharma. If one follows the *Avataṃsaka*, there are ten causal conditions for the appearance [of the Buddha];
the Tathāgata’s emergence in each case is for the purpose of benefiting others, serving as the *pratyaya* (condition) and embodying the meaning of applied skillful means.
Furthermore, the "Dharmadhātu Chapter" is both the cause and condition for oneself and others to enter the Dharmadhātu, as well as the skillful means (*upāya*).
In summary, regarding one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), both cause and fruit serve as skillful means, and both are termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Regarding the transformation of others (*para-pariṇāmana*), arising from the essence to manifest function, causing others to attain the wondrous cause, fruit, and essence constitutes the skillful means. Now, we shall merely speak of what is attained by oneself and others.
The wondrous capacity of the reality-body (*dharmakāya*) is called "expedient means" (*upāya*), and it is also termed the "dependent origination of the One Vehicle" (*ekayāna-pratītyasamutpāda*);
when this is clarified as the dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu*, the principle is fully exhausted.

Chapter Seven: The Parable of the Phantom City (This refers to the passage below where, after the phantom city has vanished, he speaks to the multitude; the commentary [Sūtra-ṭīkā] likewise places this at the end of the parable).

Regarding the phrase "the former questions and so forth," the following section provides a detailed analysis and reconciliation of the similarities and differences between the provisional and the real as they were established in the past and revealed in the present.

Why is this? Although the textual meanings explained during the three cycles of the Trace Gate are numerous, to speak briefly, they primarily clarify that in the past the Real was concealed and the Provisional was established, whereas today the Provisional is opened and the Real is revealed. Nevertheless, the underlying intent for establishing the Provisional in the past remains the same.
However, although the meaning of "revealing the reality" (*dharmatā*) is one and the same, the phrasing differs;
since the formal teaching of the three stages is now nearing completion, I shall here analyze and explain the general purport at the conclusion of this parable.
While various explanations are redundant and ultimately fail to reach a synthesis, I shall briefly clarify it herein. This section contains two parts, the first of which is the explanation.
Regarding the reconciliation of the similarities and differences between the provisional teachings of the past and [the present], there are five sections in total;

the following explains the reconciliation of the similarities and differences between the revelation of today and [the past]. This section has three parts: first, recounting the ancient interpretations; second, refuting those ancient views; third, providing the correct interpretation.

Within the first part, one first recounts the question and then recounts the answer. In the question, there are two sections: first, establishing the identity of the underlying intent; second, examining the textual evidence.
The "Differences" (vibhāga) should apply to all three cycles [of the Dharma], yet only the "chariot" and the "city" are mentioned;
this is because mentioning the chariot subsumes the vehicle (*yāna*), and thus by speaking of two, the meaning of the three is fully encompassed, as both the number and the sense are identical.

Likewise, one should have said "exhaustive knowledge" (*kṣayajñāna*) and "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*), but here "non-arising" alone is mentioned, which refers to the wisdom of the ultimate fruit (*phala*). How is this known? The text states: "The chariot is outside the gate."
Since the city exceeds three hundred [yojanas], we know that this is the same analogy. Below, the text raises three differences as a challenge:

"If the intent is the same as the parable, why is there this threefold difference in this single fruit? Regarding the statement that the chariot does not exist, it is because one seeks it without seeing it;
regarding the existence of the city, one enters upon merely hearing of it, for there is no further seeking. As for the "three," the text says there are three kinds.
Because the precious chariot is transformed into a city, it is said that "movement and stillness" are distinct: the chariot is for transport, while the city is for rest.
Thus, "existence and non-existence" differ in their substance; "three" and "one" differ in their number; and "movement and stillness" differ in their function.

Why is it that while the intended meaning of the metaphor is the same, the textual meaning still contains these three distinctions? Although this inquiry does not exhaust the matter, [it serves as a starting point].
Among these, these three are essential; since their intended meaning does not differ here, I shall directly present their words.

As for what has not yet been fully explained, it will be seen for itself within the subsequent formal exposition. Among them, the first two both rely on principle and teaching, while the last one relies solely on principle.

Furthermore, in the first two, the analogy is explained first, followed by the application to the dharma; in the third, the sequence is presented directly through the dharma. Now I shall describe this.
Answer: The phrasing of the response is easy to understand, so its meaning can be conveyed through brief communication rather than elaborate text.
Next, regarding the refutation of errors: since these various interpretations of the meaning are all incorrect, they must be examined and refuted one by one.

However, within the subsequent correct explanation, their meanings will naturally be refuted, as it is made clear that those meanings are not at all tenable; thus, it is called "difficult" (or "challenging").
Because it will be seen by oneself later on, I shall not elaborate here; since difficult arguments have already been presented previously, I simply provide the commentary as follows.
Next, the third section below is the author’s own correct explanation, which contains two parts: first, a general response to former scholars with a brief interpretation;

second, from "expedient wisdom" (*upāya-jñāna*) onwards, a literal explanation based on the essential nature. Within the first part, there are five sections; the first is a brief explanation of the actual meaning.

Regarding "existence and also non-existence," the three subsequent sections from the *Nirvāṇa of the Phantom City* (*yǒu huàchéng*) further clarify these three meanings while briefly explaining the meaning of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
From the section beginning with "the city" (*chéng*), the fifth section further clarifies the three meanings while explaining movement and stillness (*cāñcalya-sthiti*).
First, regarding the phrase "sentient beings [are] equal": at that time, because all regarded it as a treasure, they were collectively [in possession of it] according to the Buddha’s wisdom.
The "illuminating manifestation" (*prabhāsvara*) has two meanings; for now, we shall follow each from one side, hence there are two differences.

When fully complete, they are equal and prepared as explained below, hence the note says "and so forth. Next, the following three sections concurrently explain the three meanings: first, the explanation of the meaning of the chariot and the city;

second, from the "three vehicles" onwards, the explanation of the transformation of the chariots and the city, regarding the meaning of existence and non-existence; third, the question-and-answer session.

The following explains [the distinction]: if both are equally transformations (*nirmāṇa*), how are the two types of transformation differentiated? Based on these three points, there should have been questions for all of them;

however, the text omits the first two and provides direct explanations only for the third, which serves as the question. First, it explains the reason for the difference in names; second, it explains the reason for the difference in essence (*svabhāva*);
and third, it explains the reason for the difference in characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). According to this intent, [the previous section] should be understood accordingly.
The locus of inquiry should include nine points of interrogation; although the ancients provided only three, their previous statements were not exhaustive.
It is precisely because of this that we now provide these three explanations for this very point. First, according to the intent of this explanation, one should interrogate as follows:
"Since both equally manifest the wisdom of the fruit, why does this [text] speak of the 'city' while the previous [text] speaks of the 'chariot'? To offer such an explanation is incorrect.
It may be understood that "city" (*nagara*) is used as a metaphor for "cessation" (*nirodha*) because it represents the ultimate goal;
"chariot" (*ratha*) is established as a metaphor to inspire beginners and lead them out of the house. These differences arise according to what is appropriate for each case.

For the sake of the beginner, three stages are established, while for one who has regressed, one stage is appropriate. This simultaneously explains the reasons for the three and the one. Next, the following passage provides an explanation.

Regarding the statement that "the transformation is not called 'transformation,'" this should be examined as follows: Since both are equally metaphors for the provisional, why is it that the chariot is not called a transformation while the city is called a transformation?
Therefore, this explanation is offered: the chariot applies to both the present and the past; from the perspective of the present, it is indeed a transformation-city.

If one follows the perspective of the past, it has not yet been attained and thus cannot be called a transformation. Consequently, from the perspective of the present, both are transformations, whereas from the perspective of the past, neither was a transformation. This is the structural point of the text.
This is because it is so explained; that which is likewise a transformation is all that is non-existent yet provisionally spoken of as existent.

To say "it is precisely this" means that it is precisely by means of the provisional that one is led into the real. As the text says: "Once they know that [the provisional] has ceased, they are led into the Buddha’s wisdom.
This question and answer follows upon that point. The intent of the question is: if it is granted that these are the same...
Question: What is the difference between the two types of transformation and the substance of transformation? Answer: There are two layers [of explanation]. Regarding the first layer:

supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) pertain to the body, while vocal sound pertains to the mouth; the body assists the mouth. Since it is said that both speech and cities are pervasive, this is explained from the perspective of the body’s assistance.
In the subsequent layer of explanation, there is no difference from the preceding one; however, it is intended to simultaneously clarify the presence or absence of the previous explanation.
For the sake of the meaning (*artha*), this further explanation is provided. Among the three previous explanations, each contains the sense of having three interpretations;

thus, these three sections comprise four meanings: (1) the meaning of the chariot and the city; (2) the meaning of the transformed and the non-transformed; and (3) the meaning of the distinctions among transformations—these constitute the four meanings.
Excluding the [first] three, the remaining three explain the differences in name, essence, and characteristic (*nāma-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). Next, below... [the first] section.
Regarding the fifth section, the explanation of the meaning of "movement" through question and answer, it further relies upon two general meanings to interpret both movement and stillness.

In the first assembly, there is the city and the messenger; in the second assembly, there is the carriage and the messenger. These should each likewise possess two meanings. The first refers to the city and the messenger, and the one and the two.

The intention here is that they serve as metaphors for the provisional teachings (*upāya-dharma*). Why are they called a "city," a "messenger," "one," and "two"? This is based on the answers provided to explain the meaning.
The force of the argument must necessarily contain these two meanings; since this question is posed in terms of names and numbers, it constitutes two points.

Within the question, two meanings are contained: first, the question of what distinguishes the city from the messenger; second, the question of what distinguishes the one from the two. How can one single point investigate these two distinctions?
In the answer, the meaning of the city and the messenger is addressed first, which corresponds to the subsequent answer regarding the meaning of the one and the two.

These two meanings clarify the sense of movement and stillness. Initially, there should have been three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion; however, for now we shall explain the conclusion rather than the heading. The heading states:
"The 'making' is a metaphor for the teaching (*śāsana*), and the 'city' is a metaphor for wisdom (*jñāna*). The explanation states:

"Because the teaching is that which can express [the truth], and wisdom is that which can sever [delusion]. The conclusion states: "Movement and stillness. The text here is extremely concise; one must examine it with careful attention. Next, I shall explain the first point.

The two passages should also both contain the text for the inquiry and the conclusion; the conclusion merely provides a direct explanation. As for the conclusion, there is a difference because [the first] has distinctions, whereas the second has no distinctions.
First, this is explained again with emphasis, while also reconciling the meaning of the "chariot. Based on this explanation, the preceding sections should be combined into six rounds;
we are now at the sixth, which emerges from within the fifth. There should likewise be questions and answers here, and the questions should also encompass two points.
This means that "vehicle" (yāna) is one, while "expedient" (upāya) is two—namely, three and two. Why is this? It is because the formal teaching speaks of both the vehicle and the expedient.

To understand this, one asks: why are there three expedients, and why are there only two vehicles? Reflect on this, reflect on it! If this is so, whereas the ancients had only three, we now have eight; together, there are eleven instances.

Let us set forth the essentials of why these two [categories] serve to connect cause and effect. (Note: The text appears to be a commentary on a Buddhist doctrinal classification, likely concerning the *Ekayāna* (One Vehicle) and the various *upāya-kauśalya* (skillful means). The numbers refer to specific categories within a systematic analysis.)
The instruction given to people to build [the city] from beginning to end is such that "gō" (合) refers to the old city and "nehan" (涅槃) refers to the chariot outside the gate;
thus, these are all results. As for the "unconditioned" (wuwei), it refers simply to the remainder with no remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

That is to say, within the teaching, one excludes the causes and takes only the essential results; therein lie these two types. The "unconditioned" is precisely the unconditioned result within the category of results, which is the city.
For this reason, all of these pertain to the meaning of movement and stillness. Above, there were eight meanings, namely the three and the five;
since the ancients explained only those three, it is known that they did not exhaust its essence. Although they explained those three meanings, they were still not quite correct.

Now, in contrast to them, although my explanation is brief, it encompasses both the horizontal and the vertical, yet it is still not entirely refined. Below, I shall provide a more complete explanation, which will be even more so.
This is clear and also very easy. Each [verse] contains four lines, and three repetitions result in twelve lines; thus, there is no principle that is not exhausted.
Once this structural pattern is grasped, all similar cases can be categorized accordingly. The previous interpretations need not be attacked to be refuted, for they are all undermined.

Within this, the initial section provides the correct explanation, while the subsequent section concludes by showing how it differs from the old interpretations, which remain confined merely to the Hīnayāna (Small Vehicle).

This explains the meaning of how the present [teaching] differs from the old [tradition]. Now, in order to exhaustively clarify the meaning of the provisional and the real within the sutras—specifically to manifest this principle of "this very place" (ji-fang)—I have made these statements regarding distinctions and leveling. The ancients did not grasp this intent;

they merely followed the literal text to produce divergent interpretations, failing to comprehend the principle of perfect penetration. Consequently, their work resulted only in the doctrines of the Hīnayāna. You should reflect upon this well.
"Reflect upon this; reflect upon this.

Above, the distinctions and similarities regarding the textual meanings of the provisional teachings (*upāya*) from the past have been fully analyzed and explained. Below follows the intent for reconciling the similarities and differences between the current revelation of the Real (*bhūtārtha*) through the opening of the provisional.
There is a question and an explanation. First, as for the meaning of the question: although [the teachings] are identical in their opening and revealing [of the truth],...
Since there are five locations, how could there not be differences among them? This question is posed in order to reveal the Way that is without fixed direction.

In the answer, there is first a statement and then an explanation. Within the statement, there are two parts; as for the explanation, it distinguishes only one [of the five], because the meaning of the others is easily understood through this general principle and thus is not explained separately.

It should be known that the commonality of all five is simply to collectively manifest the true meaning of the One Vehicle. Therefore, they are distinguished [from the perspective of their specific manifestations].

Regarding the statement that there are discrepancies, as explained below, these are precisely the five distinctions (*pañca-viśeṣa*). One should know that these five distinctions are eternally one and the same;

yet, because these five distinctions extend even to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), this directionless and wondrous Way cannot be understood by following the text in a single direction, but must be understood as encompassing all things.
Furthermore, in the subsequent explanation of the "distinct" [teachings], there are five locations where [these distinctions appear].
Although these five distinctions do not deviate from the true path of the One Vehicle, this is a specific explanation;
the general meaning is self-evident and need not be further discussed. Nevertheless, these five meanings are simply the general and specific aspects of the fourfold "One.
This is clear in the text, yet one must understand that each of the five instances fully possesses the meaning of the fourfold "One" in its entirety.

As explained previously, we now again group these distinct elements into four broad categories. Thus, the general and the specific, as well as the pervasive and the particular, are likewise without fixed direction;

one cannot simply direct each toward the "correct" because of the singular, wondrous principle. Therefore, one must follow this approach without inhibition. Otherwise, the core tenet would become obstructed and stagnant.
Furthermore, the textual characteristics are easily discernible and do not require prolixity; thus, following the previous classification, they are applied with brevity.
There are eleven instances of provisional [teachings] here; this reveals that the ultimate reality must likewise possess inconceivable aspects.

The preceding explanation reconciles the differences between the provisional and the real across past and present teachings, which is truly essential and appropriate. If one can grasp this meaning, other cases may be understood by analogy;
one should reflect upon this well, though I have not yet had the leisure to provide a full and detailed exposition.
The Chapter on the Dharma Master (An Explanation of Entering the Text).
First, the reason for the title is clarified: it is named after the person and the teaching that cause the wondrous Dharma to circulate among oneself and others.

In the first section, both the teacher and the disciple are described as having "profound merit and heavy blessings"; some say this refers to the merit of oneself and others. For now, [we shall proceed].

This is considered to be the cause and effect. Herein, one may see for oneself that in the initial section of the commentary, within the "Gate of the Disciples," because it was not yet fully settled, it was explained from a general perspective;
strictly speaking, it should be said that the text concerning the first disciples is further divided into two parts:

first, the narrator’s account of the intention behind addressing Bhaisajyarāja; second, the passage beginning with "Addressing Bhaisajyarāja" and following, which is the Buddha’s formal exposition. Within this [latter part],...
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, clarifying the disciples during the Buddha’s lifetime; second, clarifying the disciples after his parinirvāṇa.
Within the section on the Buddha’s lifetime, there are again two parts: first, distinguishing the types of people; second, from "I have all... onwards, clarifying their merit and retribution.

Within the section on the types of people, there are further two parts: first, clarifying the human category; second, from "Of such kinds as these" onwards, clarifying the conditions for receiving their predictions. If...
To take this alone as two chapters is incorrect for three reasons: first, it is incompatible with the meaning of the current passage;

second, it does not correspond with the meaning of either the preceding or subsequent passages—the preceding being "merit is profound and blessings are heavy," and the subsequent being the second part of the passage on extinction;
and third, if one follows the previous interpretation, the meaning of the text at all three locations will be perfectly consistent. Furthermore, this serves as an analogy for extinction.

Regarding the subsequent interpretation of the passage "the preceding humans" (*qian ren lei*), the character *zhi* (至) should be understood as having the meaning of "those who are born" (*sheng zhe*), which refers to human beings.
Yet, various commentators either limit the scope to the three vehicles (*san sheng*) or extend it to the character *lei* (類). This is further untenable;
the reason for this is that the language of that time was concise and brief, and later generations, failing to penetrate its depth, have acted precipitously.
Because of textual revisions or omissions, those who study this matter should examine it in detail. Regarding what is called "categories" (*lei*), there are generally two types:
first, the general sense, which refers to broad classifications such as the third, fourth, and eighth [grounds], corresponding to the meaning of "various classes of sentient beings";
second, the specific sense, which refers individually to the three minor [perfections] within the sūtra text.
The term "flow" (liú) contains these two meanings, and is therefore called a "category" (lèi). Some say that this passage should instead be divided into three parts:

first, the category of humans; second, the recording of conditions; and third, the merit and retribution. However, I maintain that following the previous example, the subsequent section should consist of only two parts.

It is improper to further divide the text into three sections, as this would contradict the internal logic of the meaning. Furthermore, according to the *Sūtra Commentary* (Shùwén), it may also be considered as such [only two].

Regarding the second [section], the first two do not require further subdivision; however, within the subsequent commentary, the text is somewhat obscure and difficult to perceive, so one must briefly understand its beginning and end.
Now, to clarify the Great [Vehicle], there are two distinctions: first, a general explanation of the text from "one sentence, one verse" onwards;

second, a further specific clarification of the three meanings of essence and characteristics. Within the first [of these], there are three parts: first, the direct exegesis of the text, starting from "seeing... [the following].

"Truly, having already [done so]" and below, the following section distinguishes this from other sūtras. The old commentary states that the three causes below refute the specific and reveal the universal. Regarding the first of these, there are two parts:

first, an explanation that singles out the category of humans, all of whom are granted a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); next, an explanation of their merit and retribution. Within the first of these, there are further two parts: first, an explanation of the category of humans;
one verse explains this, and what follows explains the conditions for receiving the prediction. Regarding the phrase "singles out" used at the beginning: there is...
The second [term] refers to both exclusion (*pratikṣepa*) and selection (*parigraha*). Because it encompasses these two meanings, it is called "exclusion" (*prativedha*).

In the text, the first part excludes what preceded, while the latter part excludes to reveal what is now present; this is because the former is restricted while the latter is universal. The initial phrase "wondrous awakening" (*miao wu*) refers to profoundly penetrating the principle that the provisional and the real are non-dual, thereby entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
"Much-hearing" (*duowen*) refers to being fully endowed with the hearing of the three successive turnings of the Dharma wheel.
"Manifestly and deeply understanding" refers to those who attained realization through the three cycles of instruction and were thus able to receive the teaching, awakening, and entry.
"Two thousand and so forth" refers to those individuals, namely those mentioned in the "Chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecies to the Five Hundred.

Regarding the "general and specific prophecies," the two thousand five hundred are the general and specific prophecies for those present before the assembly; those not in this assembly are the general prophecies for those not present before the assembly.
The phrase "also below" indicates that the present passage both reveals and records [the teaching]. Within the text, three categories are pointed out as being together in the wondrous assembly.

The character *huà* (絓)—which also has the pronunciation *jìn* (盡), and in another reading *wùguǎ* (烏卦)—is glossed as "to bind" (*wǎn*). It should properly be read as *jìn*, meaning "to anticipate" or "to include.
This sentence captures the sense of [the disciples] already being present before the Buddha. This sentence contains two meanings, the first of which is a selection.
The phrase "after his extinction" (滅後) excludes others, as detailed in the commentary (*shu-wén*). From this point upward, it still applies generally;
from the single verse and single line downward, the three lines specifically clarify the distinction. This is precisely the causal basis for the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) currently received.

If one does not open [the text] in this way, it merely serves to identify the specific class of persons. The text is abbreviated and does not mention the meaning of "rejoicing" (*anumodana*), though its significance is actually present.
"Both" refers to the minimum; "all are as recorded" refers to the second section, which clarifies the merit and retribution.

Since the meaning of this merit and retribution is easy to perceive, the text directly cites them in summary to serve as a comparison for what follows. Within this, there are three parts: first, using the disciples as a comparison to manifest the excellence of the Teacher;
second, using the respective divisions to manifest the profundity; and third, using the lower stages as a precedent to manifest [the higher].
Zhongshang [explains] that this passage is the beginning of the section on circulation (*pravartana*), as it is specifically intended to encourage the subsequent five types of circulation.

Regarding the character "merit" (*gōng*)—that is, the three "lesser merits" mentioned previously—it can be understood that by using this character "merit," the sense of the preceding "depth of merit" is further deepened.

As for the term "complete" (*jùzú*), it is contrasted with the previous "textual brevity"; "throughout one's life" is contrasted with the previous "temporal brevity"; and the "five types" are contrasted with the previous.

The preceding section on rejoicing in the three types of action (*trikarma*) is not present in this text; these three offerings are identical to the ten types [of offerings] discussed later, as explained subsequently, hence the note says "and so forth" (*yathā*).
Moreover, since it is clear that the merit and karmic reward of these four are indeed exceedingly great, they can be understood by analogy, and thus they are not explicitly mentioned here.
Next, regarding the comparison of the shallow with the profound based on their respective categories: the reason for making this comparison is due to...
Regarding this, among the categories of the human realm, there are both general and specific types, as previously clarified in the text.

However, here we focus on the most inferior specific type to illustrate the gravity of the retribution; furthermore, because it reveals the vastness and depth [of the teaching], this explanation is necessary. Next, the following passage serves as an illustration to clarify the two preceding weeks.
This appears after the final week because its meaning encompasses the preceding ones; thus, it governs the bestowal of the teachings throughout the two preceding weeks.

The records are very few; although there were the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings during the first week, they only attained understanding and realization, yet the bestowal of predictions (vyākaraṇa) was not yet clear.

Therefore, [the text] summarizes this here to illustrate it by analogy, which is why this explanation exists. One should know that this section of text contains these many meanings and encompasses them all.
If one does not explain it in this way, how could one exhaustively grasp its most subtle and wondrous purport? Thus [it is said].
These three points regarding the intention [of the sūtra] are far-reaching; I have not had the leisure to explain them in full detail, so I trust that scholars will discuss them in detail.

From this point onward, the following is a comparative analysis of other sūtras. Since those sūtras already contain accounts of prophetic declarations (*vyākaraṇa*), if these same matters were stated again here, how would one distinguish between them? Therefore, this explanation is provided. Within it, first, the contents of those [other sūtras] are presented.
Regarding the passage recorded in the Sūtra following this, the subsequent section that distinguishes the differences may be understood as follows:

Next, the third point, based on the text which contains the words "bestowing predictions upon the three vehicles," refutes that biased attachment and clarifies the meaning of the convergence of the two [vehicles].

Since there are already predictions for the three vehicles, one knows that there are those who receive understanding through the three vehicles; thus, it is taught for the sake of the three vehicles, just like the preceding parable.
This is explained in detail within the chapter.

The preceding general explanation of the textual meaning is now complete. Below follows the second section, which specifically clarifies the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the three meanings.

Regarding the characteristics of these three meanings, they are: (1) the fourfold [joy], (2) a single moment of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), and (3) the three [factors]. Furthermore, regarding the specific explanation of these three, the Sūtra states:
These three [passages] previously provided only a general explanation of their meaning without specifying their essential characteristics; therefore, they are now further set forth.

Although these three texts serve for the time being as two [sections], the first clarifies the essence and characteristics of a single four-line verse, while the section beginning with "a single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*) explains the essence and characteristics of rejoicing (*anumodana*).

Within the first of these, there is first a general application based on other texts, followed by an illustration to reveal the specific section in question. Within the first of these, there is first a citation.

Furthermore, below this, another scripture is cited to corroborate the preceding treatise’s interpretation. Is this not also the case for the exegesis of the preceding flow of meaning? It is indeed so.
The four foundations of mindfulness constitute the meaning of the four lines. Just as with the four-line verse, there are both general and specific interpretations;
here, we follow the specific interpretation, taking its essential points to reveal the fulfillment of the meaning, rather than adhering strictly to the literal characters.

Next, "Observing the Mind" below provides an analogy to clarify the present sutra. Within this, first the [single] line is explained, and then the four lines are clarified; this is the initial section.

The reason for observing through brevity is for the sake of convenience in understanding. Although it is said that the observation is concise, its meaning actually encompasses both principle and phenomena;
this should be understood. This clarifies that there is not a single verse that is not "one," which is why all are called "one.
Since this is a teaching that clarifies and reveals, all provisional phrases and verses are identical to the Single Wonderful [Truth], and thus are called "one. This "one" is each and every phrase.
All verses are the wondrous contemplation of mind and phenomena; when one contemplates them, there are none that are not identical to the single, wondrous, true mark (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, they are all "one. This is precisely the contemplation of the wondrous teaching; as it is thus, it simultaneously encompasses both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*).

Is this not indeed essential and sublime? The commentary states "and so forth," the purport of which is roughly as follows. This concludes the explanation of "one. Below, the characteristics of the fourfold verse are clarified.
Each of the four passages cited also represents the opening and revealing of the four-line verse; because each one subsumes the meaning of an entire section, they are essential.
Furthermore, the word "etc. indicates that there are many other such categories, as fully explained in the preceding and following sections, so it need not be discussed here.
Nevertheless, within this context, we are currently dealing with the four phrases of the Trace [of the Buddha's teaching]: Opening, Showing, Awakening, and Entering.
The following is the second section, which clarifies the essence and characteristics of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). This is divided into three parts: first, the meaning of sympathetic joy;
second, the characteristics of sympathetic joy; and third, a concluding summary. The subsequent text further explains the first meaning. Why is it called "sympathetic joy"?
It is because there is as yet no practice of the three karmas or the five types of conduct, but only a single thought-moment of understanding regarding persons and dharmas. Regarding dharmas:
This refers to the opening and revealing of the dharma-gate of non-duality; "people" refers to those who together hear this wondrous teaching.
As explained in the subsequent text, the phrase "furthermore, by way of comparison" uses the retribution for subtle merit as a comparison to reveal the retribution for profound merit.

The intent of the sutra is to urge others with tireless diligence so that they may deeply admire it. The following section clarifies the characteristics [of this retribution], which has three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation.
The subsequent citation of scriptural evidence first marks two types because the mind that understands possesses these two kinds: horizontal and vertical.
Although only two meanings are marked, there are actually three, as the third meaning integrates the preceding two; thus, it is merely mentioned briefly.
Within these three, each contains four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), though the text is abbreviated: the first has only two propositions, and the second has only one.
The final two phrases mutually illuminate one another; they are not intended to be overly prolix.

To speak of "hearing the revelation" means that even a single phrase or verse of the sutra, down to a single thought-moment, is a phrase or verse of revelation—the very source by which understanding is attained.
Otherwise, one could not achieve this wondrous comprehension. This is because all phenomena do not transcend the mind. Therefore...
This is also because it excludes the external; thus, it is said that "all thoughts are provisional teachings," which means that realizing the mind is precisely the meaning of opening the provisional.
Understanding that which is neither provisional nor real is the manifestation of the real. "The Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers to opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, being able to illumine both simultaneously is the second phrase, which refers to showing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The perfect interfusion of phenomena and principle (*dharma* and *tattva*) is precisely awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*) and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. "Phenomena" refers to the provisional means of the two extremes;
"principle" refers to the reality toward which one is directed; and "perfect interfusion" refers to that which is neither phenomenon nor principle.

Because it is awakening, yet because it is the entry into phenomena and principle, it possesses four aspects. This is the opening, showing, awakening, and entering within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).

This is exactly as explained above regarding the interpretation of the four phrases through the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*). As for the phrase "although [the merit] is complete," this is cited from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* to provide a specific proof for the meaning of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).
Because one has not yet realized [the truth] through understanding, the nature [of reality] remains within the realm of phenomena; therefore, it is said thus.

The "Secret Treasury" (*biczang*) refers to that sutra—the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*—because it contains and stores the principle of the three virtues (*triguṇa*) and encompasses all myriad merits; hence it is called the "Secret Treasury. This sutra is the Buddha himself.

Because this knowledge and vision is subtle and wondrous, boundless and pervasive, and because it exhausts all discourse and leaves nothing outside itself, it is called the "Secret Treasury. To indicate its vertical dimension:
such knowledge and vision represents the ultimate limit of profundity and depth, having exhausted all principles and fully realized one's nature.

Next, regarding the horizontal dimension, as for "all mental phenomena" (*citta-dharma*), some claim that "mind" refers to the six consciousnesses and "phenomena" refers to the six faculties and six objects; however, we maintain that they refer to the nine realms of existence, including both the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*).

This refers to the provisional teachings (*upāya-dharma*). "All are Buddha-dharmas" means that they are the true dharmas of the Buddha-dharmadhātu, including both the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*).

This is the realization of the provisional in order to conform to the real. "Unobstructed" also refers to the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) as explained previously. It encompasses the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*);

namely, realizing the Buddha-dharmadhātu [is simultaneously] the nine realms of existence (*navadhātu*), and so forth—this may be inferred by analogy. Since the citation of evidence for this utility is already established:

While some claim that the citation of this sutra’s passage [in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*] was made in error, I maintain that it is likely a quotation intended to corroborate the essence, practice, and function;
yet, as for the essence itself, it is no different from what preceded, being identical to the meaning of "knowing the secret treasury.

Furthermore, if one follows the later text which opens the five grades into ten grades of faith, this also accords with both of these two meanings; thus, whether one adopts the former or the latter approach, both are valid.
Next, regarding the stage of "binding" (*bandhana*): because one can understand in this way, it is known that the point of correctly grasping the understanding is identical.
Since the Dharma is thus—meaning that one is able to realize all phenomena in this manner—the realization and understanding regarding all persons is likewise;

this is the second meaning of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), namely, both oneself and others. To "bind crosswise" means that the preceding [explanation] was based on the matters and principles of the Middle and the Extremes (*madhyānta*).
In this context, the ten realms are for the time being treated collectively according to their phenomena; thus, they are "horizontal," which refers to their breadth.
Below, the mutual identity of the horizontal and vertical is clarified by analogy with the preceding two cases, and for that reason it is so. This also integrates the preceding two.
Being profound yet identical to the broad, and being broad yet identical to the profound—neither both nor either; yet by citing only these two phrases, all four are fully encompassed. This is why...

That all are thus is because both the subject and the object are sublime. Next, regarding the citation of scriptural evidence, it serves to verify the meanings of the preceding three and four [sections].
"Little learning" refers to a single set of four lines; "much understanding" refers to the meaning of three sets of four lines.
Since these three and four lines encompass the entire treatise, they are called "much. The concluding remark "later" intends to clarify the meaning of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).

This profound and extensive [explanation] is but a brief interpretation; it will be further explained extensively later, namely in the subsequent "Analysis of Merit" (Guṇa-vibhāga), specifically within the chapters on "A Single Thought of Faith and Understanding" (Ekacittotpāda-adhimukti) and "Rejoicing" (Anumodanā).

What has been presented above is merely an explanation by way of causes and conditions (*nidāna*); the remaining three [modes of explanation] can be understood by analogy, and thus are not mentioned again.
Furthermore, the reasons for not explicitly stating the meaning of the four *paryāya* (the fourfold teaching) within the section on causes and conditions can likewise be inferred accordingly.
Now, it is said that the four concluding sections and three analogies throughout the text follow a single pattern, which corresponds to four meanings. What are these?

First, the conclusion and analogy concern the relationship between teacher and disciple within the world. Second, the conclusion and analogy concern the relative depth of realization among individuals within their respective stages.

Third, the conclusion and analogy illustrate what is below by means of what is above and middle, showing that this is not unique to others. Fourth, the final section removes the aforementioned doubts and provides an antidote. Thus, it concludes.
The summary of the essential characteristics of the [three] bodies is the primary meaning; reflect upon this, reflect upon it.

Next, regarding the explanation of the time periods after cessation, although the temporal settings differ, the textual meaning and its structural logic are entirely as before; they can be understood by analogy, so I shall not laboriously elaborate the text.

The Commentary on the Fourth [Chapter], explaining the passage concerning "attaining the proximate fruit," interprets the meaning of attaining the proximate stage through three phrases of the sūtra text.
Furthermore, there is a successive (transmissional) interpretation of the preceding intent; although there are three successive interpretations, there are only two [points]:

the first phrase corresponds to the meaning of "converting the provisional to enter the real" (*huān quán rù shí*), while the second phrase expresses the intent of "revealing the provisional and the real. As for the third...

The phrase "opening and revealing" (*kaikaku*) signifies the meaning of interpretation and manifestation; thus, the three [stages] are simply the convergence of the two meanings of opening and convergence.

Because one converges through opening, one is able to attain the proximate fruit. If opening and convergence are themselves opened, then the benefit of the three types of wisdom (*trividya*) is complete;

this is the stage of Perfect Wonder (*enmyō*), which is called "proximate" because it borders upon the True and is adjacent to the Holy. If one deeply penetrates that all phenomena are real through opening and convergence, one then realizes the Stage of Truth (*shinjitsu-i*).

Regarding Bodhi, since it has not yet reached ultimate realization even when considered in its general aspects, it is described as "near. Within the text, the three phrases are explained in detail through two stages:

first, a direct exegesis following the literal sequence of the passage; second, a further explanation based on the three types of wisdom (*trividya*). In the first stage, the initial phrase is explained first:
since it is said that [the teaching] is subsumed under this assembly, the meaning is clearly essential. Next, the phrase concerning "opening and revealing" (*kai-gen*) is explained.
This single phrase encompasses the two gates and exhausts the essential tenets of this entire sutra.

Although we currently proceed according to the immediate context, if one were to fully realize the intent of the Trace Gate (Jikimon), the method of interpretation cannot be treated with mere superficiality.

Within this, there are three major distinctions: first, the presentation of ancient interpretations; second, the questions and answers that synthesize various explanations; and third, the presentation of our own current interpretation.
This is precisely what is being taken up for extensive explanation here. Regarding the initial brief summary, there should be four schools of thought;
however, the text of one master is not in sequential order and has fallen into the subsequent section. Thus, in the present text, there are currently three.

Among these three schools, the first two merely explain the meaning of "opening and revealing" (*kaishisho*) but do not explain the essential nature (*tairyo*) and characteristics (*sō*) of that which is opened and revealed. Although the third school possesses [both],...
Although the terms "subject" and "object" are mentioned, the characteristics of that which reveals them are ultimately not clarified;

therefore, it is also not permissible to first present the explanations for each and then subsequently evaluate their validity. In the initial section, the meaning of what was previously concealed is first elucidated;

now, from the passage on the Royal City (*Rājagṛha*) onwards, the reason for its current revelation is explained. Thus, the former teaching, being applied to those below, establishes the nature of this revelation.
The meaning of this is briefly indicated below. At that time, those who criticize [the position] do so because they reject it on the grounds that it contradicts the meaning of the scriptural text.

Why is it not called "abandoning" (*he*) but rather "refuting" (*po*)? Although "abandoning" is essentially synonymous with "refuting," why is there a distinction made between them in the *Xuan* (the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*), where both refutation and abandonment are separately differentiated? To summarize the essential point: the ultimate intent [of these terms] returns to the same fundamental meaning.
Because it is singular, the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) says: "This sutra possesses only two kinds of wondrousness—the relative and the absolute"—which is precisely this point.

This meaning correctly clarifies that [the former master] failed to recognize the distinct meanings of "opening" (*kāi*) and "abolishing" (*fèi*). By using "abolition" to explain "opening," he violates the text and turns his back on the meaning.

Next, the second master’s exposition consists of three phrases: the first is the thesis, and the second is the explanation; these also clarify "opening" and "closing" through the lens of the present and the past, which is easy to understand.
Next, as for the present critic, he deeply approves of its meaning, yet it must be refuted and reconciled.
This is because each passage of the sūtra states that what was previously done by means of skillful means is now explained in this way; thus, it certainly accords with the intent of the sūtra’s text.
Next, regarding the third school: first, its two manifested bodies are set forth, and the three periods have already been described to establish the preceding meaning.
The intention is that it must be understood in this way for the full meaning of the text to be exhausted.
Although there are words of instruction, if their specific characteristics are ultimately not distinguished, what is the use of having words without a clear purpose?

There was a commentary by a former master that read "thousand" (千) instead of "one thousand two hundred" (一千二百), and he simply relied upon that as his interpretation, claiming that one thousand two hundred arhats and eighty thousand bodhisattvas [attained realization] because of this.

Because one attains awakening and understanding, it is called "comprehension" (*liǎo*). This is entirely based on the meaning of the human text and is precisely the teaching of manifest dharma (*nītārtha*).

It consists of the twelve divisions and the eighty-four thousand [teachings]. It is precisely because of failing to understand that the ten [errors] become a thousand that this sequence was established.
Now, the reviewer [notes that] the previous two schools both rely on verbal expression and are therefore merely the teaching; this [present school], however, is the very essence.
Since the former master adopts the latter approach, he adds the word "body" (*kāya*).

[The opponent] privately claims that this is not the old [tradition], desiring merely to manifest his own ability by secretly using another's interpretation as his own; thus, it is a private fabrication.
Since this is already that [opponent’s] doctrine, it is precisely the *Jiemo* (Trace) teaching; yet to simply speak of "expedient means" while adding the word "body" is also untenable.
Since his interpretation does not go beyond the characteristics of "opening and revealing" (*kaishi*), his intention does not differ from that of Guangzhai;
therefore, it likewise falls under the refutation of the meaning. Of the three previous schools, two are entirely incorrect and one is half-correct. Why is this?

Because the meaning of "opening and revealing" perfectly accords with the text, whereas the meaning of the "two gates" has not yet been manifested for themselves; since this meaning is not yet complete, it is half-correct. For this reason, it remains...
Regarding the enumeration of alternative interpretations, I shall restate the explanations of two schools concerning the three dharmas;
these should properly be moved and placed below the third master, as the textual meaning correctly follows that sequence. If they were left at the end, it would be highly inconsistent with the order.
When we reach the relevant passage, I shall clarify this further.

From the response at the end of the section on the "Gate" (Mén) begins the second assembly of the various commentaries (*shì*). This is not merely an exposition based on one's own views, but also incorporates the perspectives of others;
hence it is called the "assembly. Within this, if we follow the order [of the text] as it stands, there are four distinct parts:
first, the direct commentary on the two phrases of the sūtra; second, the refutation of the error of others who establish their interpretation by relying on the three dharmas; third...

There are two questions and answers that analyze and complete the preceding four gates. The fourth [gate] cites fifteen locations as proof to explain the meaning of what was previously termed "gates" in general.
If the second section were moved to precede this, then there would be only three [sections] here:
first, the fourth, and the third. Within the first of these, there is first a direct self-explanation, followed by citations from commentaries to corroborate it.
The text at the beginning is not very orderly; now, wishing to make the meaning of the text easy to understand, I shall arrange it according to sequence.

Within this, there are two parts: first, an explanation of the two gates; second, an explanation of the two gates of "opening and revealing. That which was revealed in the past is what is revealed now, while that which reveals it now is the present [explanation].
Regarding the first part, there is first an explanation of the gate of skillful means and next an explanation of the gate of reality. Each of these two gates [is further divided].
There are two [parts]: first the question and then the answer. The question is posed by another, while the answer is given according to one's own intention.

Following this structural pattern, if one wishes for easy understanding, there should be four layers of question and answer. First, one should establish the premise: "Since it is called a 'skillful means' (*upāya*), it must be distinct [from the goal].
The answer should be: "It is one. Next, one should further ask: "If it is a single skillful means, how can it be named a 'gate' (*mukha*)?"

One should answer by stating that there are two meanings, and then further inquire: "What are the names and characteristics of these two? One should respond by stating their names and distinguishing their characteristics;

apart from this, they constitute four [categories]. Only in this way is the full force of the meaning exhausted. Although the phrasing follows a concise style for brevity, it consists of a single question-and-answer sequence.
One must recognize the preceding structural context (*pūrvatantra*) before one can achieve comprehension, whether for oneself or for others. Thus ends the section on the gate.

These two must be understood as follows: "being able to penetrate" (*tōng*) refers to its essence (*ti*) when considered from the perspective of its own nature (*zìfēn*), while "being able to penetrate" refers to its function (*yòng*) when considered in relation to others (*duìtā*).

Its own nature is the gate (*mén*); it receives this name because it faces toward the fruit. Since it concerns the causes of one's own practice (*zìxíng yīn*) and has not yet discussed penetrating others, it is the essence.
That which is "able to penetrate" is the gate, for it is able to accord with reality; thus, it is the function. If there were no...
In the past, when one considers the essence itself, one cannot comprehend the present; yet, since the present and the past are discussed in conjunction, these two [essences] must necessarily exist.
One should especially reflect well upon this. The phrase "the essence itself" and what follows below explains the characteristics of these two essences.

Within this, the six characters beginning with "for the sake of reality" (*tattva*) are superfluous and useless, as the two gates are fully explained in the main text; thus, the subsequent text does not follow a sequential order.
Later generations, failing to understand this, forgot these annotations and thus did not employ them.

Although the initial passage correctly identifies the source, that which is cited is from the *Entry into the Dharma Realm* (*Gandavyūha*) chapter of that same sutra, where Sudhana seeks spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

The phrase "various kinds" and so forth serves as a general heading, while "counting sand" and so forth provide specific illustrations. Counting sand is a method of calculation, just like the six arts (*ṣaḍvidyā*) of this land.
Among the various arts, this is the middle one; "zhong" (中) may originally be written as "nòng" (弄) or "bì" (抃), but it should be taken as "suàn" (算, calculation).
"Guanhai" (觀海, Contemplating the Sea) refers to the Dharma-gate of penetrating the ocean-like qualities of the Buddha, as explained in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* regarding the eight virtues of the sea.

Because there are many such categories, the word "etc. (*deng*) is used. This constitutes the differentiated conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which causes sentient beings to enter the Path through these initial stages.
The term "taking the essence" (*dangti*) does not refer to penetrating the true reality (*shixiang*); rather, it refers to the meaning of taking [the teaching] as its own essence.

This is the "taking the essence" of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), which borrows the "One" to manifest the various [teachings] by analogy; thus one may properly evaluate its intent. Although this meaning appears frequently in later passages where it is explained, there is no need for it here.

"Taking the essence" means that through skillful means (*fangbian*) one attains the meaning of skillful means, and through the ultimate truth (*zhenshi*) one attains the principle of the ultimate truth.
Yunmen can only pass through [the gate] because it is merely named a "gate," hence it is called "the very gate" (*jimen*).
This second explanation regarding the opening of the text under these two gates is out of order;
it should properly be placed later, beneath the section explaining the two gates of *dharmatā* (true reality). Its placement here is incorrect, causing students to exhaust themselves in vain.

The realization of effort is firm; next, the second [point] explains below how it is able to penetrate this, for there is no separate dharma entirely other than that which takes the preceding as its substance and functions as a gate.
This substance and this gate are precisely the function of the preceding gate; otherwise, the textual structure could not be harmonized, which is easily seen.
Next, in the explanation of the "true aspect" (*dharmatā*), the word "also" follows the analogy of the preceding provisional gate.
"Yi" (亦) means "also. Initially, if one does not embody the non-obstruction within the essence, one cannot realize it for oneself, nor can one respond to others.
This is also the gateway of reality (*tattva-dvāra*), the cause for personally realizing the truth. Some say that this gateway is identical to the previous one;
however, I fear this may not be the case. The two scriptures cited by my reflections clarify the meaning through analogy, and the principle is precisely as stated here.

The second is the "principle" (*li*), which is that which is penetrated; the "gate" (*men*) is that which penetrates, which is to say, it is the function. This is as detailed in that sutra and should be sought according to the method.

Regarding the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there is both the phenomenal aspect (*shi*) and the noumenal aspect (*li*); following the previous example, this is also the noumenal aspect. The "gate" is likewise the cause.

What is explained by these two is the entry into realization through one's own practice (*svayam-bodha*); because it is contrasted with the entry into provisional [teachings] below, the explanation of the "function of penetrating" immediately follows when considering the substance itself.
Taking the entire body [of the teaching] as this gate of universal penetration (*sāmānya-praveśa-mukha*), it is easy to see that the above section concludes the explanation of the two gates;
the passage below explains the meaning of "opening and revealing" (*kai-shi*). Therefore, the text following these two gates should properly follow immediately after this point.

Regarding the "two gates," this refers generally to the two gates of the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*tattva*); it does not mean specifically referring to the capacity for universal penetration within the provisional gate itself.

Regarding these two as being "two," no commentator has failed to err. Why is this? Although there are two aspects each for the provisional and the real, these constitute merely the two gates of the provisional and the real;
by citing these two, all four are subsumed. Therefore, it is improper to designate them separately as distinct texts.
To provide separate interpretations based on the order of the text is a grave error; may you examine this carefully. Within the provisional, there is only one aspect of opening and closing.

The meaning of these words—that the opening and closing of the gate of reality is likewise—is easy to perceive. This concludes the explanation of the two phrases from the sutra text cited in the main commentary.

Below this, the commentary cites the interpretations of the sub-commentators (*ṭīkā*) to briefly clarify that their intent is the same; it first explains the two gates and subsequently explains "opening and revealing. First:

In the middle section, each merely takes up that which is capable of penetrating, without speaking of the actual substance itself; first, it clarifies that the real penetrates the provisional, and next, by "drawing upward," it clarifies that the provisional penetrates the real.

Thus, the meaning of this gate is distinguished. The term "efficacy" (*kō*) refers to the power and function, which is made manifest. The phrase "it is not... and so forth is an explanation of the textual structure, which is easy to perceive.

Therefore, in the previous clarification of the gates, the real was presented first and the provisional second; subsequently, in the clarification of the opening [of the provisional], [the same order is maintained].
