After these three, one then returns to explain these three dharmas to others. The reason for there being exactly three is that the method and principle reside solely in these three;
they must not exceed nor be deficient. It is essential that these three be so.

This is precisely as found in the questions and answers within the initial commentary on a single dharma at the beginning of this chapter. In the text, first the three virtues (triguṇa) are explained, and next the three...

The commentary on the *Guan* (Contemplation) explains that the third chapter is cited later in the text to reveal its meaning; thus, the four assemblies’ prior textual passages share this same significance.

As for why the first three virtues are explained [here], these three virtues are precisely the Great Nirvāṇa (*mahāparinirvāṇa*), while the subsequent chapter is titled "Peaceful and Joyful Practice" (*anurakṣita-śānti-caryā*).

In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, "peace and joy" is precisely the Great Nirvāṇa, as it correctly clarifies that propagating the sūtra is the cause of Great Nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is also named the Tathāgata.
"Practice" refers to the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa; since these three are all termed "Tathāgata," they must be explained by way of the three virtues (*guṇa*).
As for the subsequent explanation by way of the three norms (*vidhi*), a norm is a rule, and the meaning of "rule" precisely clarifies the method for propagating the sūtra.

One should distinguish between the similarities and differences of the virtues and the norms; the three norms are established by taking the aforementioned three virtues as the basis. This concludes the first part of the explanation.

Each [of these] possesses all three aspects: first, because they possess the wondrous virtue of perfect penetration and being without limit; "guidance" (gui) refers to the rules for propagating and proclaiming the Dharma.
To cite the subsequent chapter: the "Peaceful Practices" (Anle Xing) are precisely these three natures.

"Practice" (xing) is cultivation within this context; thus, cultivation and nature manifest one another. The meaning of returning to the broad exposition is as previously explained, following what was set forth before and after.

Regarding the preceding passage, the previous commentary stated that both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are present; yet here it speaks only of the "robe," for if even a single item already possesses these three aspects, how could there be only two?
The previous section used "carrying on the back" and "shouldering the load" as metaphors for the essence and function of the Middle Way.

The explanation in this sutra text is also very brief, because since the previous section provided a comprehensive explanation, one may understand the present case by analogy. Next, as for the five benefits, they arise precisely from reverent compliance.

Because he practiced the Dharma, he has reached this state; this is an expansion upon the various merits and rewards mentioned previously. Furthermore, within the subsequent "Peaceful Practices" (Anrakugyō), it is explained even more extensively than here.
Seeing the Great Assembly of Equality within the Jeweled Stūpa refers to the subtle and boundless nature of the two wisdoms—the provisional and the real—which accord with the wondrous realm.
Because the realm and wisdom are perfectly harmonized and complete without deficiency, all Buddhas are equal.
This wondrous person’s *prajñā* is the Dharma realized by the wondrous persons of all Buddhas. The metaphor of the single city gate represents the supreme and wondrous Dharma;
the metaphor of entering from all four directions represents how the Buddhas of the three periods of time equally realize this Dharma. The meaning of the finger-pointing is likewise so:

one must skillfully understand its intent, for there are both general and specific aspects. This specifically takes up the uncommon *prajñā* that accords with the limits of the perfectly wondrous path.

To speak of "not" does not mean to point exclusively to that specific school; or, regarding those who doubt the three gates being distinct, one simply takes up their differences and similarities without necessarily insisting on a fixed position.
Furthermore, the four gates—expedient and real, existence and non-existence, and so forth—all equally testify to the single principle.

Moreover, since there is no divergent name that does not equally testify to the wondrous Dharma, all four directions enter [this truth]. If we consider it in terms of persons, the Śākyamuni Buddhas of the three periods of time are themselves these four.
Furthermore, since each of the two sūtras possesses two names, they each consist of four phrases; while the essence of what they convey does not differ, there are four distinctions.
The essential meaning here is precisely to clarify that the substance is identical while the names differ;

thus it is said that the single dharma of Prajñā is spoken of with various names according to the different capacities of sentient beings, as seen in the seventeen names. Moreover, when one constantly speaks of the different names of Prajñā, it is not necessarily restricted to these four.
This very meaning should be understood as taking up the entirety of the "unshared" (asādhāraṇa) while still remaining relative.

Within this context, two interpretations may be offered: that of persons and that of dharmas. Regarding persons: throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions—horizontally and vertically—there are four directions.

Although the persons in these four directions differ, they realize the one principle without distinction; thus, while the substance manifested by the dharma-logic is one, its names are manifold. The "four directions" here serve as a metaphor for names.
The "differentiation" refers to the single city, which is the very essence of that which is expressed.

One should know that the eleventh chapter, "Seeing the Jewel Stūpa," is named according to the relationship between the agent and the object; "seeing" is the agent of seeing, while the jewel stūpa is the object seen, as clarified in the sutra.
The stūpa manifested so that the great assembly might behold it together; it was from this that the name was derived. The "Chapter on the Stūpa" (Shèpǐn) is divided into two parts:

first, the title, and second, the text. The title has four modes of explanation. First, regarding the etymological translation (yīnyuán), there are two sections: first, the transliteration, and from "from the Āgama" (*āhán*) downwards is the second, the explanation of the meaning.
Within the first [section], there is the translation, the distinction, and the two names; both "tá" (stūpa) and "tōu" (thūpa) are terms produced in ancient times.
The sound is the same, but because the translators differ, there are these variations in translation.
These have also been rendered as two different names in this land (China), both of which are approximations based on partial resemblances; they do not yet capture the essential reality.

The Sui translation says "Great Accumulation" (*mahāstūpa*), while the recent translation is not entirely correct. The new term is *stūpa*, which means "highly manifest," referring to its physical form.
The translation by Gao Li Zhuxu is clear and distinct, exactly as in the scriptural text. It manifests the supreme sage’s honored and manifest virtue and morality;

because its form is majestic, it causes beings to turn their hearts toward it in reverent admiration, thereby attaining the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*. Hence it is called "highly manifest" (*gāoxiǎn*).

Furthermore, the phrase "also below" serves to distinguish [it from others], as there is a difference between existence and non-existence; thus there are two names. *Cetiya* (支提) is likewise an old term.

The explanation that "it also emerged" is not entirely correct; according to the standard Sanskrit, it should be *caitya*. Therefore, all translations produced in recent times have taken this as the correct term.
Furthermore, the character "zhī (pronounced 'duo')" in the phrase "the branch-name of the second meaning" is a corruption of the pronunciation of this same *caitya*.

From the section on the *Āgama* onwards constitutes the correct explanation of the meaning. However, the sutra merely asks about the causes and conditions for the three matters: the emergence of the stupa (*tā*), and so forth.
Since the Buddha provides a comprehensive response without discussing the name or meaning of the *stūpa*, I shall now directly translate the name and explain its origin based on four points.
This is not an explanation of the name or meaning of the *stūpa* itself; as the meaning was briefly clarified above, it is not the intent here, and thus is not discussed.
Among these, the first serves as proof that this sutra is [the teaching] of all Buddhas.
1. Because it is a jeweled stūpa of the Dharma-body; 2. because it serves as a witness to the profound and vast benefits of this sutra; 3.
because it is specifically intended to cause those with karmic conditions—both present and future—to sever doubt and give rise to faith through these two gates; 4.

because it is specifically intended to clarify that this sutra can manifest the inconceivable, wondrous virtues of the three bodies of all Buddhas. These four points collectively encompass the three [sections] within the sutra.
The causes and conditions for this matter are largely as follows; that is, the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*.

First, since it is revealed that this sutra is the locus upon which the stupas of all Buddhas of the three periods rely—just as the *dharmakāya* relies upon its objective realm, which is like the *bhājana-loka* (the vessel-world)—this constitutes the *loka-siddhānta*.
Next, since the profound and vast merit and benefits of the sutra are specifically elucidated, giving rise to wholesome roots, this constitutes the *sukha-siddhānta*.

Because it is the ultimate [of the three], it constitutes the second [meaning]. Since it can both realize what precedes and initiate what follows, and because it is capable of removing doubt and engendering faith, it constitutes the fourth [meaning], which is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Because it reveals the wondrous path of the three bodies (*trikāya*), it constitutes the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). The remaining three meanings are easy to discern.

Regarding the category of the antidote, there may be much confusion or error; I hope you will examine this with great care. Do not assume that merely because this text refutes the ancients, it must therefore constitute the antidote.

Regarding the treatment [of these], why is it that among these four, only the "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*) is mentioned? This is primarily intended to accord with the Sūtra and refute ancient [interpretations].
It should be presented here; it would not be appropriate to introduce it later at the beginning of the Sūtra.

Following the eight negations, in the explanation of "equal great wisdom," the questioner intends to distinguish between the similarities and differences with the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. Why? Because that [Sūtra] is named *Mahā*...

Regarding the statement that "the two names for 'Great Wisdom' (Mahāmati) are identical," how can their two essences be the same? This is because one seeks the identity or difference of the two essences based on the identity of the two names.
As for citing the *Śāstra* as an explanation, it is because that treatise specifically explains the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

Since that [treatise] refers to it as the "Exquisite Dharma" (*Saddharma*), the essence is the same. However, according to the titles of both works, the names are different; yet, according to the texts of both, [they refer to the same reality].
That which is praised within [the text] is precisely to manifest that their essence (*tattva*) is identical. Below, the analogy of a single city is raised to clarify this identity of essence;
that all four directions enter it is a metaphor for how different names signify the same single essence.

Furthermore, if one were to correlate this with the four gates or what has been realized by the Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions, it would also be possible; however, for now, we shall rely simply on the principle that while the names differ, the essence is identical.

Other interpretations would be too prolix, so I shall stop here; one should seek them further in the treatise itself. However, since this [explanation] is stated according to the meaning of the "unshared" (asādhāraṇa), it is called "common" (sādhāraṇa);
if considered from the perspective of what is "shared" (sādhāraṇa), they are entirely different. One must properly grasp the intended meaning so as not to fall into error or confusion.
From the passage "There are some who divide... onwards is the second explanation of the chapter's text. Within this, first, the divisions and sections made by ancient scholars are recounted.

It is not that [the structure] is established only later; rather, in correctly analyzing the beginning and middle, one first describes the structural outline (*kośa*) and subsequently clarifies what is untenable.
Furthermore, there are minor omissions within the text; that which has not yet been explained is not adjacent to the preceding or following sections.

Some say that the first phrase refers back to what follows, meaning the seventeen chapters, because the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* did not exist in antiquity; the second phrase, conversely, refers back to the preceding ten chapters, namely the Introduction (*Nidāna*).

The passage "from this chapter downward" up to the end of the "Dharma Master Chapter" (法師品) is further clarified by another commentary, which states that the characters "eleven" (十一) are an error and should correctly read "seven" (七).
This refers to the seven chapters starting from this current chapter down to the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit" (分別功德品).

The section following Maitreya’s questions refers to everything from the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (隨喜品) to the very end of the scripture; thus, both the *Shu* (Commentary) and the *Ji* (Record) are in error.
Now, regarding this second explanation: all of it concerns the taming and ripening [of beings]. Which three chapters are these?

The "Emanation" (*nirmāṇa*), the "Life Span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*), and the "Distinction of Merits" (*guṇa-vibhāga*)—these three chapters are all spoken by Maitreya, extensively presenting his requests, to which the Buddha then provides the formal exposition and speaks at length.
If this is so, why then judge them as being the body-wheel of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-kāya-cakra*) and the subsequent sections as being [the wheel of teaching]? This is below.
The Wheel of Speech takes correct exposition as its body and circulation [of the teaching] as its mouth;

given that this is the meaning of the "Dragon Master" (Nāgārjuna), and since the preceding text states that "the reality is far-reaching while the chanting is near," should we then leave this Wheel of Speech as being incorrect? Now, I say that this explanation is somewhat incomplete;
if one were to fully account for the substance, the original and correct version should state: "The eleven chapters below constitute the third [section], categorized by..."

The Wheel of the Body reveals the original and the trace within it as two; the first four chapters and a half constitute the revelation of the original and the trace through the Wheel of the Body of Supernatural Powers.
From Maitreya’s question downward is the revelation of the original and the trace through the Wheel of the Mouth of Dharma-preaching. It should indeed be understood in this way.
The reason we know it is so is that this is the interpretation of the masters such as Longyin and Yaoyao in the preceding text; therefore, because of this...
Within the second [section], the provisional and ultimate aspects of the body, there are naturally three parts. This first phrase, stating "eleven," generally enumerates these three;
specifically, it refers to the first two parts: the introduction and the main body.

The introduction refers to the initial emergence of the bodhisattvas from within the "Emergence" chapter (*Niryūha-parivarta*), which is also termed the "wheel of the body. From the question [of Maitreya] onwards is termed "Maitreya’s Inquiry," which is—
The "Oral Wheel" (*khuṇḍala*) is also called the "Section on Entrustment" (*parindanā-parivarta*); that which follows constitutes the third part, the Section on Circulation (*parivarta*).
Since its meaning is easy to understand, it is not described here in detail. How is this known?
I have seen Master Yao’s work, in which he also explains it through ten points. Regarding Master Yao’s interpretation, it says: "Master Yao [received this] from the Jewel Stupa."

From the conclusion of the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (Ṛddhi-paṭala) onwards, it clarifies that the provisional and real aspects of the body still involve skillful means; the direct teaching itself is thus expanded into three [bodies].
Furthermore, I have previously seen an ancient manuscript of this commentary by a former master which states here:

"The first four and a half chapters concern the Wheel of the Body of Supernatural Power, which reveals the fundamental and reveals the traces; the remaining text is identical to this [present version], for it is indeed the reality. It is for this reason [that the division is made].

Therefore, we know that the fixed [number] is as stated previously; all other [interpretations] are erroneous. Some say: "Since there was originally no *Dadata-parivarta*, how can one speak of 'four and a half'?
Now, I respond: this subsequent [classification] is a comprehensive explanation based on meaning. If [a category] is absent, it is already implicitly included within the count.

Furthermore, while one should have spoken of the body in terms of the provisional and the real (*upāya* and *bhūta-artha*), why does one speak of the fundamental and the trace (*mūla* and *liṅga*)? The intention is to clarify that the provisional and the real are precisely the meaning of the fundamental and the trace.

Since the preceding chapter on the "Original and Traces" (*honji-suijaku*) is also termed the "Provisional and Real" (*gon-jitsu*), it is known that this meaning extends to clarify the provisional and real nature of the body itself—that is, the original and trace aspects of the body.
Therefore, these are manifested through alternative names. First, regarding the "Wheel of Supernatural Powers" (*abhijñā-cakra*):

as for the term "wheel," it refers to such events as the sudden emergence of the jeweled stupa, the distant gathering of emanated bodies, the three transformations of the pure lands, the opening of the stupa, the taking of seats, and the reception of the assembly into the void.
Countless teachings from within [the scripture] suddenly emerged in the air, and the fourfold assembly all saw them filling immeasurable space;
such matters as these are all the workings of the wheel of the supernatural body (*ṛddhi-kāya-cakra*).
Therefore, the first four chapters and a half constitute the application of this wheel of the supernatural body, which initiates the dialogue and correctly explains the provisional and the ultimate.
The "expedient means of the wheel of speech" (*vākcakra-upāya*) is simply another name for the "Introduction" (*nidāna*).

From the "Chapter on the Emergence" (*Abhyudgama-parivarta*) and the questions of Maitreya onwards, that which belongs to the explanation of the wheel of speech is entirely unknown to those who do not understand the boundaries of this textual division.
Alas! Such is their intention; however, if one were to discuss its esoteric meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*), it would be self-evident that they are currently incorrect.

My own interpretation is not so; I believe that the "Chapter on the Emergence of the Vision" (*darśanavyūha*) appropriately fits the context of this matter, and thus it would be premature to rely on [the former] as the primary basis here.

Based on this, one should follow the previous enumeration of three [categories]. Fearing that later students might not deeply penetrate the meaning of the text and thus fail to discern between the right and wrong of these two paths, I have recorded my critique of them.
Let all learned scholars examine this with care and deliberation, and do not speak of it hastily.

Regarding the intent behind the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna appearing to listen to the sutra: first, the treatise (*śāstra*) is cited for explanation, followed by the Master’s own explanation. The meaning of the treatise can thus be understood.
Some may ask: "Why did Nanyue [Huisi] deviate from the sutra? Now it is said that Nanyue was precisely expounding the intent of the treatise and therefore did not deviate from the sutra.
It is further said that although both explanations each possess their own logic, when compared with the ultimate meaning of the sutra text, they are ultimately not yet fully consistent.

What has been attained is as described in the aforementioned *Dharmabhāṇaka-sūtra*: the essence and function [of this teaching] are praised in various ways as being lofty and vast, and its benefits are profound and great.
For this reason, the Honored Treasure (the Buddha) first received these five kinds of wondrous benefits;

consequently, he made a great vow to go to every place throughout the ten directions to realize and manifest them, so that all beings might likewise share in these wondrous benefits. This is the essential purport for the circulation of this sutra. Furthermore—
This is the profound method for initiating the fundamental stage. If one relies on the treatises and their commentaries, it is truly impossible to harmonize with the sutras;
yet if one relies directly on the sutras, it is very easy to harmonize, whereas relying on the treatises makes it extremely difficult to penetrate.
For now, it is appropriate to follow the easy path rather than the difficult one. For this reason, it can be understood that the Great Master Tiantai did not pursue further verbal elaborations.
Thus, you should reflect upon this well. Chapter Twelve: Devadatta. Regarding the commentary on this chapter, there are two parts:
first, the title; second, the text. Within the title, there are three sections: first, a brief explanation of the title; second, the discernment of bodhi; [and third, the explanation of the chapter].

Regarding the existence or non-existence of "Sa" (薩) and its placement after the word "ren" (人), this first section provides the formal explanation of the name and clarifies the purpose of its inclusion.

Within this initial part, it is either written in white characters or provided as a commentary; since the original text mostly uses the character for "note" (注), it should indeed be read as such. As for the term "causes and conditions" (因緣), this is said in general terms;
it refers specifically to the causes and conditions of worldly response and resonance, which is simply the meaning of the world (*loka*). This is why it is "hot" (熱).

Knowing that there will be destruction, one feels sorrow for the benefits of the Buddha-Dharma; this is the "person. Its fundamental purpose is to eliminate the feverish affliction (*saṃtāpa*) of sentient beings;
this is the "remedy" (*pratipakṣa*). To remove the fever of sentient beings and cause them to attain coolness (*śītalatva*) is the "ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*).
The remaining two intentions can be understood from the subsequent text, which explains them further, as well as from what is discussed in the *Record* (*Ṭīkā*). Thus it is.

This is still an old translation that is not entirely essential; it should properly be rendered as "Devadatta" (the first character, *tié*, is pronounced "tiān," meaning "heaven"). It means "bestowed by heaven.
Because his parents prayed to heaven and obtained [this child], they attributed the merit to its source, saying it was bestowed by heaven; thus he is called "Heaven-Bestowed" (*Tiānshòu*).

During the Kaiyuan era, there was a Brahman monk named Śikṣānanda, which in the language of Tang means "Capable Bestower" (*Néngshòu*); from this we know that "Datta" does not [itself] mean "bestowed."
Since this heat was already said to have been bestowed by Heaven, how much more so when it is added that he has manifested his traces; there must certainly be four meanings.

That the parents obtained this through prayers to Heaven is the worldly meaning of cause and response (*loka-artha*). That Heaven bestowed it upon him to inspire his holy transformation and bring great benefit to others is the meaning for the sake of humans (*puruṣa-artha*).
And that he manifested retribution for his past transgressions so that immeasurable people would not dare to commit such acts is the meaning of restraint.
The perverse and evil are precisely what the remedial intention can greatly illuminate; it manifests the Sage’s transformation so that immeasurable people attain the Way.

This ultimate truth (paramārtha) exists because of these four causes and conditions; therefore, Devadatta is able to practice non-Dharmas and penetrate the Buddha-way—this is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).
Having long realized the ultimate truth, he is also able to long perform this function; this is the relationship between the original and the manifested (honji-suijaku).
To cultivate wondrous contemplation based on the wondrous principle of nature is to give rise to wondrous wisdom; this is precisely the contemplative wisdom bestowed by Heaven (*tiānshòu*).

Thus, the significance of these names and meanings is extremely essential. Next, regarding the phrase "Master Rui’s nine tracks" (*jiǔzhé*), it means that various schools all claim that Master Róng employed them as nine tracks.
It is well known which is correct, yet one should understand that their differences are not of urgent importance.

Fortunately, there is no stubborn adherence [to a narrow view]; otherwise, everything is as explained in the commentary. One should understand that regarding this chapter, the title and the substance are both general and specific. Why is this?

Within the text, it fully clarifies that two people—past and present—benefited through the universal application of the sutra; yet the title refers only to the single person at the time of the initial departure.
Thus, one knows that while the substance is general, the title is specific. Nevertheless, since they are equally exhortations for practice, the title cites one example to represent all.

Furthermore, what limitation could there be? To explain: regarding the subsequent explanation of cause and effect, the reason this section is the most extensive and detailed is precisely because it describes the nature and characteristics of how the World-Honored One, in the past, relied upon this sutra to cultivate wondrous causes and thereby attain wondrous fruits.

This was done so that future generations might believe and uphold it; thus, it must be so. Within this, one should know that the classification according to the teachings is merely relative (paratantra). Each point should be understood accordingly.

All must be opened up and made free of dependence in order to fully exhaust the purport of this sutra; know this, know this! When the Dragon Girl appeared and prostrated, the text says she praised [the Buddha] with verses.
Many people harbor doubts, asking: "Is this praising the Buddha, or is it self-praise? Now, what is the source of this doubt?
If one says it is praising the Buddha, why does the Commentary state that it clarifies how upholding the sutra leads to liberation? If one says it is self-praise...
Is there any principle in praising the Buddha by means of self-praise? Now it is said that this is precisely because one takes the understanding attained for oneself and uses it to praise the Buddha;
the commentary explains the reason for this, stating: "Why is this clear?
As in the *Avataṃsaka*, the various classes of beings all describe the Dharma-gates they themselves have attained to praise the Buddha, for the Dharma-gates attained by oneself are entirely..."
Because it is that which the Buddha has realized, it is used as a praise; now this is also like that. To clarify what one has attained for oneself, one uses the wondrous path praised by the Buddha;

by using the Buddha’s praise, one reveals that what one has attained is no different from the Buddha’s, because by initiating this, one will subsequently become a Buddha—reflect on this, reflect on this!
One should say "I have heard" (*śruta*) and then say "I uphold" (*dhārayāmi*). This is not the "upholding" among the five [precepts], but correctly clarifies [the meaning].
Having realized the wondrous Way as it was heard, because that realization is forever free from regression or decline, it is called "upholding" (dhāraṇī);
this clearly demonstrates the realization itself. Regarding the statement "accomplishing the two bodies," these are the two bodies of the True (Dharmakāya) and the Responsive (Nirmāṇakāya).
However, the descriptions of the Buddha’s bodies in various sutras and śāstras differ; for instance, the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states that Śākyamuni is named Vairocana.
Vairocana is simply one essence with different names. Some speak of two bodies, as the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states:
"All Buddhas equally possess two kinds of dharmakāya, namely the true reality body (*tathatā-kāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).

Some speak of three bodies, namely the dharma-body, the reward-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), and the transformation body, as extensively taught in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and other sūtras and śāstras. Some also speak of four bodies, likewise as in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, which says:

Regarding the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, Nirmāṇakāya, and the ten bodies—as taught in the ten fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, and the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*—their respective lifespans will be clarified later.
Although these accounts differ, they are merely variations of combination and separation according to the needs of the occasion;
thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "It should be known that the ten bodies are subsumed within the three bodies, for the three are essential. This present text [is likewise].

In this context, only two bodies are explicitly clarified, yet they inherently possess the four true bodies—namely, the Dharma, Reward, and Response bodies, which include both the superior and inferior aspects.
Although these four are complete, they are essentially reduced to two: that of self and other, or essence and function. If expanded broadly, they become immeasurable;
yet if one seeks the ultimate essential, they are but one. This is what is meant by the "wondrous body," and thus it is said that its meanings are immeasurable.
The Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous Dharma-body is such that one is all and so forth; thus it is said that it can manifest everywhere throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
Now, this passage specifically clarifies the essence and function of self and other as its essential point, and for this reason, only two are mentioned.

These two correspond to the robe, the seat, and the chamber: the robe and the seat represent the true essence, while the chamber represents the functional application. Their separation and union may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the eight aspects of knowing speech (*jñānavāk*), the text mentions only two, which are simply an abbreviated mention of two among the eight. However, they ought to be complete as eight;
since the duration [of the teaching] is so long, how can it be said that it occurs "immediately"? The wondrous Way is boundless—how could there be anything distant?
The *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that within each single aspect all other aspects are fully present; since its wondrous function is boundless, why would this not be possible?
However, according to the *Extensive Commentary on the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, it is clarified that each manifested body possesses two meanings:

first, manifestation as a response (*saṃdarśana*) throughout the beginning and end of a single lifetime; second, transformational manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), which is non-existent yet suddenly appears.

In this present case, it may be either a transformational manifestation, which has these two aspects, and because they follow one another, they are merely referred to as "eight. If it were a manifestation as a response, the meaning would be as previously explained; both meanings apply.

"Do not communicate with worldly sentiments; as for the statement that 'views and speech are merely equal,' this means that upon hearing the sutra within the ocean, one immediately realizes the Buddha-body.
Upon emerging from the ocean, at the boundary of the transformation body, one proceeds to the south;

it is said thus because one teaches solely by means of the dragon girl's body. As for 'expedient skill' (*upāya-kauśalya*), it refers to the arising of wondrous function immediately upon attaining the wondrous essence."
The passage below reveals his essential body, which is none other than the Samādhi of the Universal Body; it is merely another name for the Wondrous Samādhi.
To identify this as "expedient skill" (*upāya-kauśalya*) does not mean that he was originally an expedient person whose function was skillful means.

Thus, the *Mūlakarma-sūtra* states: "Upon hearing this sūtra of stainless great matters, one immediately attains wondrous enlightenment and becomes a Buddha in the ten directions.
If it were as you have explained, what would be the purpose of hearing this sūtra? Furthermore, the preceding section intended to extol its subtle and wondrous nature.

If there were those who, upon hearing this for even a brief moment, could immediately attain ultimate Bodhi—though such words exist, no such person has yet been seen—Mañjuśrī emerged from the ocean to clarify that such persons do indeed exist, thereby providing proof for this meaning. He asked:
"Is there any sentient being who, by practicing this sutra, can quickly attain Buddhahood? He replied: "There certainly are," and briefly cited one as an example.
To manifest all that is correct, it is revealed that the essence of this sutra is perfectly sublime and its power and function are swift;

yet it enables those who are ordinary and inferior to attain the state of superior-rooted sages. It refers precisely to those whose vehicle-zeal is intense while their precept-observance is lax, as fully explained in the preceding text. Thus, there is no room for doubt. However—

"Having heard the Great Dharma, they have all attained the Way; what causes and conditions led them to be born in my palace, and by what causes and conditions did they all hear the Dharma and awaken to the Mahāyāna Path?

This passage clearly demonstrates the principle of "slackness in precepts but urgency in the vehicle" (*śīla-śithila-yāna-tīvra*), and it is firmly trustworthy;
thus, there is certainly no room for doubt regarding the karmic causality of the dragon girl. Even the jackal in the *Avadāna-śataka* belongs to this same category. (End of quote)
"Please consider this well. Some say that his attainment of Buddhahood is partial, while other commentators calculate it differently;

However, we maintain that this merely conforms to human sentiment and does not capture the essential reality. Why? Because the sūtra has two aspects; from the beginning, it should have been titled "Receiving and Upholding" (Upadhāraṇī). From... [text continues].
Subsequently, they should be named "Exhortation to Maintain" (*dhāraṇī-anuśāsanā*) so that each obtains its own portion; otherwise, the integrity of the whole is not yet complete.

To maintain one [aspect] is to encompass both, whereas to add two [aspects] results in the loss of both excellences. It is essential to prioritize the spirit of faith. If one speaks only of "maintaining," it generally encompasses both; why is this so?

Because "maintaining" is general, while "exhortation" and "admonition" are both specific. The title of the sutra precisely captures this essential point, and the commentary is naturally [consistent with it].

If even those who study this commentary are thus confused, how much more so will those of other schools? As for what is called "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*), it does not refer to the "receiving and upholding" (*udgrahaṇa*) among the five types of practice;
rather, it refers to the totality of the five types and all practices that enable the teaching not to fall into decline, and is therefore named the "Chapter on Upholding.
The rest is as explained in the notes and is easy to understand. Within this, there should be the fourfold meaning of *siddhārtha* (the four purposes), which includes "upholding" and...
Taken together, "receiving" (*sei*) refers to the world (*jigai*), "honoring" (*hō*) refers to the human (*ninjin*), and "exhorting" (*kan*) refers to remedial action (*taishō*);
these lead one to realize the wondrous Way, the primary meaning (*daigi*). This is very easy to see; do not fail to recognize it yourself.
Chapter Fourteen: On Peaceful Conduct (*Anurakṣaṇācaryā*).
Regarding this chapter: from one perspective, it refers to the Dharma; from another perspective, it refers to the agent and the object—that is, it causes sentient beings to cultivate this practice.
This, then, is an expansion upon the previous two aspects of agent and object. The title of the chapter should properly be rendered as "Cultivating the Four Peaceful Practices."
"Practice" (*caryā*) signifies the relationship between the agent and the object; it is named directly after that which is performed.

Furthermore, while there are both general and specific meanings of "four," because this refers specifically to the "four [aspects]," it is named directly after the general sense (and so forth). Regarding names derived from the Dharma, there are both general and specific types.

As for the specific type, it is named after the Dharma of the wondrous cause and effect that flows and circulates. "Peace and Bliss" (*anurakṣa*) refers to the wondrous fruit, and "practice" refers to...

The term "wondrous cause" (*miaoyin*) further carries the meaning of distinguishing the general from the specific while manifesting the particular. This is because the names "cause" and "effect" are generally applicable, yet here they are used specifically to manifest the wondrous.

Furthermore, regarding the principle of the general and the particular, one should say that these four lines on "peace and happiness" proceed directly from the general while implicitly containing the particular, just as in the previous case of the title of the "Dharma Master Chapter. contemplate this, contemplate this! Furthermore, there are two general approaches to explaining these chapters: by way of names and by way of the text. Since the present section differs somewhat from others, it is divided into five parts:
explaining the names, the purpose [of the teaching], the sequence, the essential nature, and the explanation of the text. Now, [I shall explain]...
Regarding the five essentials, there are only two parts: first, the explanation of the titles (of the four chapters), and second, the explanation of the text (of the final chapter).
Within the explanation of the titles, the method of exposition is further established, which consists of three sections: stating the number, listing the names, and providing the explanation.
The statement "three" refers to explaining this title by means of three methods. Upon examining the twenty-eight chapters thus explained, only four categories are employed therein.

Furthermore, the structural form of this concise and extensive exposition is particularly distinct from others, as the essential methods for the benefit and edification of the final age, conveyed through this single section and two gates, are entirely contained herein.
Therefore, it is for this reason that the Great Master commanded practitioners to necessarily recite this chapter; there must surely be a basis for this requirement.

Since it is essential to be thus, how could one manifest it without the essential method? Thus, one must clarify the essential method, followed by listing the names of the essential matters—namely, the three karmas as the substance, the preceding and current chapters as the function, and the three types of assemblies as the gate to the essence.
Furthermore, "Matters" (*vastu*) comprehensively encompasses the four matters from beginning to end within this chapter;
the "Textual Gate" refers to the passages consisting of two locations and three phrases. These are the essentials taught in both this treatise and various other sūtras.
The reason for selecting these three is that the title itself precisely accords with these three essentials, and by means of them, the textual meaning of the entire work is largely exhausted.

Based on these three, there are two brief and extensive explanations; the first may be reduced or increased. Next, the explanation proceeds with further brief and extensive divisions, each of which has three sub-divisions.

This refers to the three types of action (trikarma) being free from transgression—namely, ten for the body, four for speech, and four for the mind.

To advance is to contemplate these four modes of the three actions as practices for propagating the sutras that benefit both oneself and others. Because they are named according to the cessation of activity within these three actions, it is said thus.
Regarding the sequence of contemplation attached to the text: if it is of the superior grade, then the three characters represent the three virtues (triguṇa) together.

their specific meanings are contained herein, just as the verse on bodily conduct fully possesses these three. These three...

First, it is appended to the preceding chapter precisely because these three characters of the title are the very meaning of the three passages concerning clothing and so forth.

because he is clothed, the Dharma-body is at peace; this indicates that it is indeed this body, and not any other. Since the Dharma-body is thus at peace...
The physical body is naturally at ease; this specifically clarifies that it is the Dharma-body which is being cultivated, hence the term "ease. Within "bliss" (*sukha*), there are also two meanings:

This title is easy to understand from the text itself; although the phrasing differs in two places, there is no distinction in their sequence or meaning.

This meaning is consistent with the previously mentioned "gate of the reality of the essence. As for the text, it most clearly reveals the meaning.
This is done for the sake of brevity. Within this, there are two parts: first, the sequential assignment of the three characters to the three gates; second, their sequential explanation.

if it were attached to the second section, it would likewise have to be attached there as well. Therefore, it must have been added by later readers and was not originally so. The preceding matter is generally summarized.
Regarding the three types of karma, the meaning was previously explained by way of their cessation and performance; subsequently, it was explained by way of their substance according to the text.
Now, this dharma-gate appears to explain the meaning primarily by way of its function, while also concurrently relying on its practice;

therefore, it is called a "dharma-gate. As for "immovable," it refers to the Immovable Samādhi; thus, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states: "The greatest samādhi of all Buddhas is named 'Immovable. This means:
The ability to subdue all demonic adversaries and attain the Unsurpassed Way is entirely due to this power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Therein lies the Lord of Immovable Vajra; he presides over this gate and is able to shatter all demonic obstacles. He is also named "Invincible," as his power and function are most supreme.
"Non-acceptance" refers to not accepting the three grounds of Māra; that is to say, this power of meditative concentration is able [to overcome] all...
One does not cling to any state—whether good, evil, or neutral. "Non-practice" refers to the Samādhi of Non-practice (*apracāra-samādhi*).
This "practice" carries the meaning of "proceeding," yet this concentration can penetrate the fact that all phenomena are originally thus; what further destination could there be?

The sequential explanation of the textual meaning is presented clearly. Within the first section of the explanation, there is the formal exposition, the citation of evidence, the presentation of scriptural passages, the illustration through metaphors, and the conclusion.
Next, in the explanation of "delight" (*sukha*), the first phrase provides the title without yet explaining its meaning; please reflect upon this carefully.

The meaning and characteristics follow in sequence. The subsequent section explains why [the first stage] does not experience [feeling]; below that, it concludes by explaining how the name is obtained. First, regarding the non-experience of the five kinds:
these five types of feeling constitute the measure of that non-experience. Ordinary persons—that is, those outside the Way—should not possess suffering, pleasure, equanimity, sorrow, or joy;
thus, they fall within the four propositions and the ineffable. Because they transcend the five [stages] of the three teachings, [this stage is established].
The phrase "up to and including" (乃至) means that the two characters "not receiving" (不受) above govern the five [categories] below.

Regarding the explanation of "giving rise to views" and so forth, there is both a general and a specific sense. The specific sense explains the "not receiving" of the five aspects of the Perfect [Teaching].

Since one does not receive the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), one likewise does not receive "non-receiving. Why is this? Because those who cling with emotional views cannot attain entry [into awakening].
This also clarifies that the absence [of suffering] is what is called "non-experiencing" (*anupādāna*). Conversely, the absence of suffering is what is called "bliss" (*sukha*).
This concludes that the absence of both suffering and bliss is termed "bliss," and that "great bliss" (*mahāsukha*) refers to the permanence of bliss.

Therefore, the *Eighteen Emptinesses Treatise* (*Aṣṭadaśaśūnyatā-śāstra*), in its explanation of the four virtues (*catvāri guṇāḥ*), follows this sequence for its conclusion. Next, regarding the explanation of "non-action" (*apravṛtti*): first, non-action is explained, and subsequently, action is explained.
At the beginning of this section, first, by citing the preceding example of the absence of reception (*anupādāna*), it is shown that there is no practice (*apracāra*).

Next, the extent of non-practice is clarified. Previously, not receiving was established as the cause for joy; here, non-practice is established as the basis for practice. Intending to clarify practice, one first clarifies non-practice.

Since non-practice arises from the prior state of not receiving, this is illustrated by that precedent. This clarifies that not receiving is itself non-practice; only through non-practice does [true] practice arise.
Regarding the statement that "one who is able to practice does not practice," the following clarifies what it means to "not practice. This refers to the meaning of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:

not practicing the two extremes but practicing the Middle Way. The character "practice" (*xing*) used here to conclude this section carries the same significance as the phrase "the practice of a bodhisattva" in that sūtra.
Thus far, we have briefly explained the three sets of three, which also constitute four sets of three meanings, appended to the text for the sake of structural coherence.

This is because there are two [reasons]. First, the general [classification] establishes the names based on the three types of karma—abstinence and performance; second, it establishes the names based on the cultivation of the three virtues and reliance upon the three modes of conduct (*triyāna*).

Since the latter three are gates, they are established based on the causes. Because these three sets of three are combined to establish the name, it is called "Peaceful and Joyful Conduct" (*sukhavihāra*).
Reflect on this, reflect on this! Next, as for the extensive [explanation]: these three sets of three constitute nine dharmas that bind [the practice together].

Since it is impossible to provide a complete account of all the points involved due to their vast extent, one must first summarize them and then elaborate upon them again; only then can they be fully understood.

Finally, regarding the extensive section on the Dharma-gates, although the text does not provide an explicit explanation, it merely sets forth an exhortation; yet even so, the underlying meaning cannot differ from what has been stated.
The first three [sections] constitute the cultivation of the three preceding causes to attain the three fruits; therefore, they are called the "Three Dharma Gates.

The reason for this is that while the original title of this chapter concerns the meaning of the causes and fruits of *nirvāṇa*, the previous brief explanation merely served to gloss the three characters of the title and had not yet precisely clarified its essential tenet.
Therefore, at the beginning of this extensive exposition, it clarifies the causes and fruits of *nirvāṇa*, even though they have already been addressed.
Because the essence of cause and effect was not yet known, the following section clarifies that each of these causes and effects has three aspects to manifest their reality.

This is the actual exposition of the "Three Refuges," for if one can diligently practice them, one will swiftly attain entry [into the path]. Subsequently, the three dharma-gates are further expanded;

since the ultimate purport reaches its limit here, it is called "expanded. If one does not grasp this essential purport, then even after exhausting the literal commentary, there will be no [realization].
Regarding the contemplation of benefit, there are two parts to the initial broad exposition: first, the presentation of the headings; second, the actual broad exposition.
Within this actual exposition, there are four sections. First, the demonstration of the correct meaning: this refers to the names consisting of three characters.

From the various other [passages] below, the second section distinguishes what is not [the case] to clarify what is and is not; thus it is established as non-blissful. The final one concludes that this Great Chapter applies to all three.
Now, when "according to reality" (*yathābhūta*) is mentioned, it takes the sense of "perfection" (*pariniṣpanna*) as its proof.

Next, following the text in detail, there are three sections: first, the formal expansion of this practice; second, the convergence of the meanings of the two sutras with what follows;
and third, the interrogation and analysis through questions and answers. Within the first section, the formal expansion, there are six parts: first, citing the previous title, "Nirvana";

second, a brief explanation of cause and effect, each having three meanings; within these, there are both the presentation of numbers and the listing of names; and finally, "stopping the practitioner" and so forth.

the cause consists of the purity of the three karmas and the six sense faculties, while the fruit is named the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) and so forth, and may also be termed "Buddha-knowledge."
