Possessing all things that cannot be fathomed by others, the wheel of grasping revolves in succession without end. This contemplation below concludes by returning to the fundamental source;
this is the intended meaning of this sutra. Within it, there are five phrases: the first is a general heading, the next three explain it, and the last one provides a concluding summary.
The heading states "non-discrimination. The following three phrases explain the meaning of what cannot be discriminated; the first two phrases provide this explanation.
The first sentence clarifies that all phenomena and all persons are themselves the blissful person and phenomenon, and there is nothing further that is not blissful.
The latter sentence clarifies that all practices are themselves the practice of nirvana, and there is nothing further that is not so.
This final sentence summarizes and returns to the fundamental source; it is this very wondrous cause and effect.
Furthermore, regarding these three phrases: the first appears in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, while the latter two appear in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*.

There is no need to elaborate further on the text of this chapter, as the wording differs while the meaning remains the same; since this has already been briefly clarified, the meaning will become manifest upon entering the text itself, so I shall not labor with redundant writing.
Next, regarding the reconciliation of the meanings of the two sutras—namely, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—both sutras clarify that this practice is *nirvāṇa*.
Since *nirvāṇa* is itself peace and bliss, it is clear that the practice and [the fruit] are identical and not different. Although the phrasing differs, the meaning never diverges for even a moment;

yet fearing that those who do not understand might fail to see this, it is necessary to reconcile them. Within this, first the general points are reconciled, and subsequently the specific conditions are reconciled.
This is because both sutras contain both general and specific expositions. First, within the general exposition, he first indicates that the two sutras are identical.

Next, he explains their convergence and concludes that they do not differ. Within the explanation, he first cites what is taught in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*: "the Tathāgata’s practice" is precisely this "practice of peace and bliss.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Tathāgata," he explains the convergence by showing that the former refers to the person, while the latter refers to the dharma; for the person and the dharma are mutually identical.

"Not different" (*abhinna*) is a collective statement; "collective" (*sāmānya*) refers to the general, while "distinct" (*viśeṣa*) refers to the specific. The collective refers to the person and the dharmas, while the distinct refers to each of the three aspects.

Furthermore, because it is said that the person and the dharmas are mutually identical, it is called "collective. "Not different" is precisely "identical" (*tulya*). To say that the distinct is also "not different" means that the distinct is likewise identical.
This first provides a general heading, and subsequently, this clarifies the following explanation which brings them into accord.
Within the middle section, there are first three [passages] and later five; within the first assembly of these three, there are first the individual entities and later the collective name.
Within the first of these, there is first the presentation of these three individual instances, followed by the clarification of the primary assembly that corresponds to those individuals.

Those three passages are all analogies, as can be understood from the commentary (*ji*). The subsequent invocation clarifies the collective name; that invocation refers to the meaning of the aforementioned three instances. Invocation.

These are precisely those three meanings; there is nothing beyond them, for they are the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Their virtue is that of the Great *Nirvāṇa*, because it is the ultimate perfection.

Fourth, "without remainder" means that these three aspects are what all Buddhas of the three directions and three times have equally cultivated, realized, and entered as the wondrous pinnacle, with nothing superior to them;
thus it is called "unsurpassed. Therefore, while the names differ, their essence is one. Next, the five distinct [meanings] will be reconciled; this is easy to see and need not be detailed.

The "Exalted Conduct" (*ārya-caryā*) that is indicated but not explicitly explained refers to the convergence of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) within ultimate emptiness; this is the seat.

The "Celestial Conduct" (*divya-caryā*) refers to arising in accordance with the natural principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); this is the robe. The "Brahma-conduct," "Infant-conduct," and "Sick-conduct" refer to this very chamber.
As for the chamber: it signifies compassion (*maitrī*). Because compassion can bestow upon all beings the two kinds of goodness—the subtle and the manifest—joy; therefore, it is Brahma-conduct.

Because compassion can uproot suffering, it is itself the illness; thus it is said that although the phenomena differ, their underlying meaning is always the same, as they are identical to the practice of Great Nirvāṇa.
Below follows the third section of questions and answers for clarification: first, two differing views are presented, and subsequently, the former view is refuted.

In the "Alternative Response," first there is a brief clarification that equally challenges their partiality; the principle of non-difference must necessarily be explained extensively below in four sections.
Since the preceding [sections] each possess two meanings, they each possess four.
Following the text in this manner not only applies to the present sutra, but also fully encompasses the texts of both sutras; it does not merely apply to the primary themes of both.
This also encompasses both meanings; the reason for its expansion is precisely due to this. Consider it, consider it.
Next, the third section on the "Three Dharma Gates" merely expands upon the three gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which are also the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣa*):

namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Furthermore, emptiness is cessation (*śamatha*), signlessness is insight (*vipaśyanā*), and wishlessness is great compassion without objective conditions (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*).
Regarding the "Three Dharma Gates": because these three gates are the union of the subject and the object, they are termed the "Three Dharma Gates.
The general meaning of these three points is roughly as explained previously and can be understood through reflection; therefore, it is omitted here.
One should consider that this chapter is titled the "Chapter on Peaceful and Blissful Conduct" because it summarizes these three sets of three, providing both concise and detailed designations.

The following clarifies the second intention. The text of this chapter consists of four lines; however, as the title follows the general explanation from the preceding sections, it likewise follows that general approach.
From here below, the three intentions combined clarify this meaning. Regarding the beginning, the chapters are first presented.

In the initial section on the circulation [of the teaching], the five preceding chapters constitute four major divisions, and this present chapter corresponds to the fourth, clarifying how those with a beginner's mind may propagate [the Dharma] in the evil world of the final age.

The person who recites this sutra clarifies its methods; therefore, it is said thus. Although the preceding passage clearly indicated the beginning, it was not yet possible to fully comprehend or realize it;
hence, this section explains it extensively. Next, the text correctly clarifies that what follows first excludes what is not relevant to this practice.

As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* fully elucidates the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*), here they correspond to the five ranks and the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). These five ranks constitute the initial stage within the beginning.

Because it is the "beginning," it is called the "initial mind. Within this, the first [point] distinguishes the person; the following four meanings distinguish the intention that it is not for whom [the teaching] was intended.
These four meanings are as explained in the *Record*. The section beginning with "In this turbid world" concludes [the previous point], for it is not what was previously mentioned.

Next, the text correctly reveals for whom [the teaching] was intended. This also first indicates that the person is afflicted by the turbidity, and below, it clarifies the reason why [the teaching] is not for those who possess the aforementioned four [defects].

Because it is the meaning [of the teaching], it serves as that which causes affliction; since it is afflicted, there is no benefit for oneself or others. Thirdly, this concludes the section on persons and explains the reason why this chapter was brought forward. Regarding the second point, the three intentions:
first, the subtle [explanation], followed by the detailed exposition. The reason for providing this subtle explanation is due to the two preceding and succeeding sections of the sutra.
The meaning of what was stated above is not fixed, as it reveals that the Way has no fixed direction; I shall now clarify this. Therefore, this subtle point arises.
In the subsequent explanation, first the lack of fixed direction is clarified, followed by the clarification of the "provisional single mode. Regarding the first:

since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is that which is expounded by the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*), it constitutes perfect practice. How could it be fixed as "one"? It is precisely because it is "one-and-all" that it is inconceivable and cannot be [fixed].

Next, the section on "Samādhi" clarifies that [the teaching] is both non-existent and yet existent due to causes and conditions. First comes the teaching, then the practice; likewise, first others, then oneself.

In all cases, the sequence is clarified first, followed by a concluding summary of the lack of fixed order, which is easy to see in the text. Below this, the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold standards) should be applied.

From here on, the fourth section concerns the essence [of the four immeasurables]. This directly cites the scriptural text to indicate their number and explain their characteristics without listing their names, because it is not known what these four things are;
therefore, they must be set forth. What was clarified previously was not non-existent, but it was a general discussion of their meaning without clarifying their specific distinctions.
Since the name "peaceful bliss" (an-akuśala) applies generally to all four, it now serves as the specific designation for each.

This correctly elucidates the essence of the four practices; therein are three sections: first, the presentation of the ancient interpretation; second, the account of the explanation by Master Nanyue;
and third, the correct elucidation of the present master’s interpretation. The first section has three parts. First, regarding the "two emptinesses," this refers to the initial practice of the body:

"not discriminating between male and female" refers to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and "all phenomena (*dharma*) are conditioned" refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Unconditioned phenomena, whether real or unreal, are all non-existent; this is precisely the dharma of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Because of this textual passage, these two types of emptiness constitute the essence [of the first stage].

Next, the three [stages] are as explained in the Sūtra, and therefore they likewise constitute its essence. Regarding the next master’s statement that there is "one emptiness": previously, in contrast to the object (*ālambana*), it was called "two emptinesses";
here, from the perspective of the subject (*ālambaka*), it is called "one emptiness. The subsequent three stages are also direct [applications of this principle].

Following the sequence of the sūtra text, the third school [teaches] that distancing oneself from all evils corresponds to the ten forms of affliction (*daśa-kṣobha*), while gradually approaching the principle of emptiness corresponds to the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The latter three [schools] are easy to understand. Although this present school does not yet fully accord [with the ultimate meaning], it is superior to the previous two.

Next, Master Nanyue correctly interprets the initial passage, which states: "While having no practice regarding phenomena (*dharma*), one contemplates all phenomena as they truly are (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*)."

Because one does not engage in [the four misdeeds] and does not discriminate [between them], this very thing constitutes its essence. Having already verbally renounced the [four] misdeeds, one ceases from verbal conduct by stopping at those four misdeeds;
thus, this is its essence. Regarding "revering those above," the text says: "One gives rise to the thought of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as compassionate fathers and teachers.
Regarding "assisting those below," the text says: "One gives rise to the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings."

This substance constitutes the fourth [nature], which is easily understood from the sutra. If these four are viewed from the perspective of the wise, they merely represent one aspect of being free from faults and have not yet fully exhausted its reality;
therefore, it is further explained below so that its essence may be completely exhausted. Next, the Great Master’s interpretation is presented:
first, the essence is formally identified and enumerated; second, its meaning is explained. In the first part, only the names of these factors are listed.

As for the various commentators, it need not be stated that their shortcomings can be known of themselves; how much more so when one further explains their meanings, reconciling them with reason and the text to fully realize the Buddha’s intent.
Their exegesis is exhaustive in its principles and consummate in its excellence—how does it compare to what was said previously?
Hereafter, even those who comment will find no equal, let alone one who surpasses them. May the wise examine this in detail.
As for what these aspirations are: *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), as well as compassion and loving-kindness, are that which guide the three types of action (*trikarma*);

the vow is that which is guided. Since these constitute the four forms of bliss, they must possess both substance and function. If there were four [functions] but no three [substances], there would be nothing to guide;

if there were three [substances] but no four [functions], there would be nothing to be guided. If there were neither four nor three, there would be neither the guiding nor the guided. If there were four but no three, it would not be the practice of bliss. [Therefore, both are necessary.]

There are three [factors] without four, and three have no place of return; the three and the four require one another, for it is impossible to lack either. Therefore, there must be both three and four.
These three constitute peace and happiness (*sukha*), while the four constitute practice (*caryā*). If there are three without four, there is peace and happiness without its cause.
If there are four without three, practice is not peaceful and happy. How so? This is because the three guide the four practices; these three are the capacity.
The essence of the guide consists of four [factors], while the essence of that which is guided consists of three. If these four and three did not exist, then the capacity of the four would not exist;
if the four and three did not exist, then the four would also be useless. Therefore, because the three exist, the cause for peace and happiness exists; because the four exist, the result exists.

Relying upon the three, one gives rise to the four practices for peace and happiness; relying upon the four, one manifests the peaceful and happy nature of the three practices. This is the cultivation of their characteristics.

Waiting for this, it exists; here, cause and effect are mutually dependent. Furthermore, regarding the three as "mind-only" (the subjective) and the four as "the three karmas" (the objective), because these objects are distinct, there must necessarily be this relationship between the subjective and the objective.
Thus, the three [kinds of] subjects that lead [to action] and the four types of objects are all present within the text;
they will be seen by entering the text itself. As for the mention of "vows," it is as explained in the fourth of the four previous interpretations.
Since all [Bodhisattvas] take compassion (*karuṇā*) as their very essence, how could it be further categorized as something merely "guided"?
This is not only unacceptable to other schools, but even within one's own tradition, it is not tolerated. Now, how can this ignorance be so profound?

Every part of this school speaks of arising from the vow based upon compassion; moreover, the sūtra text itself explicitly states that compassion is clarified first, followed by the vow. It is not merely... [the case].
If one is deluded regarding a single doctrine, one is likewise deluded regarding other teachings; this scriptural passage is indeed a profound source of confusion. Why is this so?

Because while compassion resides in the mind, the vow pervades the three karmas. Furthermore, the compassionate mind consists of only two [aspects], whereas the vows and the three karmas comprise four;
this is because, based on each of the two [aspects of compassion], two vows are respectively generated. How could such distinctions be considered as one?
Question: Regarding the latter three texts, how does one know that the first is the body (*kāya*)? It is known because it follows form (*rūpa*) and precedes sensation (*vedanā*).

Having reflected on this, the subsequent explanation of "intention" (*manas*) refers to the explanation of "formations" (*saṃskāra*); thus, the four formations must take these three as their primary basis.
Within this, the first part extensively explains the body, while the conclusion provides an analogy to reveal the remaining three formations. What is the reason for this?
One should first provide an inverse explanation and then subsequently clarify it in its direct order. That is to say: if these three were absent, there would be no great benefit;
because they are present, there is great benefit. What is their absence? What is their presence? To explain their absence is perilous suffering;
because they are present, there is great peace and happiness. The text contains both of these meanings, which are now extracted. What constitutes "great benefit"? First, it is explained:

Because there is the practice of cessation that can depart from the two extremes of ordinary beings and sages, as well as from the causes and effects of birth and death, the following section next clarifies the causes and effects of the three virtues of *nirvāṇa* that can be accomplished.
First, not falling into the state of an ordinary being means being free from the causes and effects of *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth and death);

not falling into the stages of the Three Vehicles means departing from the causes and effects of *pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa* (transformative birth and death). Next, regarding the ability to accomplish the middle [virtue], first, one is able to accomplish the three [virtues].

The causes for the great *nirvāṇa* of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*)—namely, cessation (*śamatha*) and practice (*bhāvanā*)—are able to accomplish the fruit of the great *nirvāṇa* of the three virtues.

From the first of these two cycles, one can accomplish the three virtues; next, one can accomplish the three tracks (*tri-yāna*). These are the track of the supporting accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), the wisdom-virtue of the track of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-yāna*), and the abandonment-virtue through which that [wisdom] is realized, which is the true nature of the *dharmakāya*.

The text states: "The supporting accomplishment" refers to the track of supporting accomplishment; "the wisdom-virtue supported" refers to the track of contemplation; and "that which is penetrated" refers to the abandonment-virtue.

Principle (*li*) is the true nature, the *dharmakāya*. Because it is that by which [virtue] is obtained, it is named "virtue" (*guṇa*); because it serves as a standard for other phenomena, it is the "rule" (*vidhi*). This refers to the essence and function (*tǐyòng*) upon the level of fruition.

The following is the conclusion of the section, showing that the physical action (*kāyakarman*) serves as an analogy to reveal the remaining three. Regarding the statement that "physical action is peaceful and blissful conduct":

one who is able to distance themselves from the two extremes—the causes and effects of birth and death—is practicing that which is not perilous or painful. Thus, it is called peaceful and blissful conduct.

Because one attains the causes and fruits of the three great nirvāṇas, this is the practice of peaceful dwelling (*sukha-caryā*). When the bodily action (*kāya-karman*) is perfected, the other three bodies are likewise so;
since all others are thus, it says, "it is also like this. Having grasped this essential meaning, there is no need for prolixity; I trust you will reflect upon it well. Question:
Since the bodily conduct is already sufficient, what further use is there for the subsequent explanation? Answer: There are four points concerning the application of conduct.
Because one is all, it is said that it is not the time for practice.
Next, within the text, it says: "If asked by a practitioner of shallow capacity, [the Buddha] would not speak of it because he is naturally able to do so. Thus we know this to be the case.
Although the Sūtra merely provides a general enumeration of the numbers without listing their names, and the commentary likewise does not indicate the reason why, [it is as follows].
It is precisely because the meaning of the preceding four cannot be treated as partial titles that they are not mentioned explicitly;
rather, the four themselves encompass the three as previously set forth, which fully exhausts this intent. In the first section, it says "the place of practice" and "the proximate place";
this explains these two [categories] within the initial section itself. The commentary text is abbreviated and should properly state: "The long section constitutes two."
This refers to the dual heading and individual explanations which together explain these two meanings without dividing them into two chapters; perhaps the first [chapter] has been omitted.

Alternatively, it is said that the following section provides the formal explanation, and the dual heading is found therein. Within this, there are first three traditional interpretations presented, followed by a detailed refutation of those while simultaneously revealing the correct meaning.
Regarding the initial phrase "inner ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth, it simply refers to the sequential stages of the Mahāyāna.
The "teachings" refer to the three stages of the worthy ones (*śaikṣa*) prior to the grounds. Furthermore, "beginning practitioners" refers to those from the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) onward;

alternatively, it may include those of the ten faiths (*daśaśraddhā*) as well, collectively termed "beginning practitioners. "Gradually approaching" refers to the ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmanā*), which are close to the true principle of the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*).
Moreover, the citation of scriptural evidence serves to verify the meaning of the second "near stage" (*upaniṣad*); this constitutes a sequence where the former is profound and the latter follows.

The "shallow" [level] also possesses these two meanings, and is therefore called "approaching practice" (*caryā-pratipannaka*). The second master explains it according to two meanings, both of which are shallow first and deep later;
these constitute the two meanings. Furthermore, the "object of wisdom" (*jñeya*) merely explains the meaning of the essence of cause and effect being reversed.

Regarding the third school's explanation of "practice," from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) upward is the stage of clarity; many people of ancient and modern times have referred to "stages" (*bhūmi*) as "abodes" (*vihāra*).
The section beginning with "Also, the essence of mind" clarifies the meaning of practice (*caryā*). Because practice is transcended within the principle (*tattva*), it is called "essence.
The phrase "having already passed beyond the stage of fragmentation" further clarifies this by way of location. Next, the explanation of the "near" [stage] begins;

from here downward, the stages of the near are clarified. The "non-arising" has not yet been explained. From these two points below, the explanation is concluded: for this reason, they constitute the four types of practice.

This is the first of the three [sections] within the middle [part]. Following this, the meaning of "proximity" (*upaniṣad*) as explained in these three locations should all have the word "near" (*jin*) pronounced with the upper tone (third tone).
My private opinion is that what follows below concerns the secondary form and does not clarify the correct meaning. Within this, there are eight sections in total:
the first four specifically distinguish the incorrect views, while the latter four collectively clarify the correct meaning and simultaneously reveal their errors. First:
In the middle section, the preceding three are collectively condensed into two, because the three meanings are in fact just two.
When it says "the first school," it refers back to the previous two schools. Next, regarding "both": since they are mutually shallow, they cannot be said to manifest mutual depth;

nor, since both are mutually non-existent, how could "both" be the case? This refers to the preceding chapter, namely the Chapter on Holding (*Dhāraṇī*). If both were shallow, there would be no reason to distinguish them.
Because these two are merely skillful means (*upāya*) and not the ultimate reality, neither can be established as the sequence.

The following four sections constitute a combined refutation based on the three correct principles, as there are further three points; thus, they cannot be definitively fixed. First, the refutation based on the two meanings of mutual identity:

since both "practice" (*caryā*) and "proximity" (*sāmantaka*) are modes of progression, the distinction lies only in being direct versus extensive. Next, the specific refutation regarding the methods.

Furthermore, the refutation of non-difference consists first of a refutation based on the identity of the two meanings regarding practice; second, a refutation based on the non-difference of the two meanings regarding method;

and third, a refutation based on the mutual manifestation of non-difference regarding phenomena and principle. These collectively refute the previous four positions, which cannot be definitively established. Next, to briefly reveal the correct meaning:
although the refutations are exhaustive, the underlying significance has not yet been fully clarified; therefore, it must be further addressed.
There is an inquiry that resolves the connection; first, the words of the inquiry are set forth:

"If those [previous] three meanings are not distinct, why are there further three separate explanations, each containing two meanings—namely, 'principle' being brief and 'phenomena' being extensive? "Arrival" (*yī*) means relying upon or taking refuge in;
"proceeding" (*qù*) means directly relying upon principle to clarify the process of proceeding. Furthermore, because this is a brief exposition, it is called "practice" (*xing*).
When comparing the passage concerning the "first station" (*prathama-sthāna*) with the subsequent passage concerning the "near station" (*upaniṣad*), this is indeed the case.

Those who say that "that which is based on phenomena" (*vastu-pratisaṃyukta*) refers exclusively to the ten afflictions (*daśa-kṣobha*) as being "phenomena," while the other two are not, or who claim that the first two are "phenomena" while the last one is not, are correct in their intent;
for the Sūtra itself concludes by designating the former two as the "near station. Now, upon examining the text, there are three [points].

Both are "matters" (*vastu*). Why? Because within *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), both the internal and external as well as the three types of action (*trikarma*) are fully contained; thus, they are all matters.
Since "secluded places" refers to the external, and it further encompasses both body and speech, it constitutes the matter of the three types of action.

As for *prajñā* (wisdom), since it speaks of contemplating all phenomena (*dharmas*), this involves contemplating both the environment and the inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), and it reveals the principle through the eighteen spheres (*viṣaya*). This was not extensively discussed previously.
It is said that this is not a matter of [actual] entities; it is named "attached to entities" (*pratītyasamutpanna*) because it summarizes these three types of cultivation.

As for the passage concerning the "three entities," since it is the most extensive compared to what precedes it, it serves as a broad conclusion. Regarding the statement that there is no "shallow or deep," this means there is no distinction between the four preceding concentrations being shallow and [this one] being deep.
The three above all rely on correct principle to manifest the whole collectively, rather than specifically refuting the first three concentrations individually. The latter is the most [extensive].

In the final instance, they are not different yet different, and though different, they are not different; even unto these four propositions, which differ from one another—the ancients have consistently determined their relative depth and shallowness. Reflect upon this, reflect upon it!
The following section is the second part, which provides a detailed explanation of the initial sphere of practice (*caryā*).

Within this, first the method of explanation is indicated, and then the text is analyzed according to that method. Regarding the first point: it means that by analyzing [the text] in terms of three dharmas, the method is revealed;
furthermore, one must reach the third [dharma] before its full force and number can be manifested—hence the statement. Having thus indicated the number, [the analysis proceeds].

The names [of the three] should have been specified separately below, but they are not mentioned because they are easy to understand. What are called the "three" are precisely the first, second, and third [categories] below.
This also refers to the one truth (*satya*), the two patiences (*kṣānti*), and the two truths, which constitute an explanation based on these three dharmas.
The reason for explaining it by means of these three is that it is essential for the interpretation of this specific passage. Why? Because of the text...
It says "the place where clouds move" and again "abiding on the ground of patience. Both "place" (之處) and "ground" (地) are that upon which one relies;
this reliance is precisely the principle of truth (*satya*). Furthermore, these terms must generally be explained in relation to the Single Truth (*ekasatya*).

Yet, it further states that although patience is a single truth, the objects to be endured must necessarily be twofold; therefore, it must be explained in terms of the Two Patiences, which correspond to the Two Truths (*dvayasatya*) as found in the text.
It is clear that a single truth must necessarily exhaust its principle through three aspects; therefore, it is necessary to explain it by means of the three truths (*trisatya*).
Only in this way can its full force and numerical scope be exhausted; thus, these must necessarily be these three dharmas.

However, one should know that each of these individually comprehensively accounts for the entire text and must not be separately divided into three distinct sections. Furthermore, the explanation of the first section itself is further divided into three sub-sections.

This is a separate analysis of the text. Within the explanation of the three [categories], it is further divided into three parts: first, the formal explanation of the three; second, the summary and reconciliation of these three dharmas as "this is named...";

and third, the summary and return to what was explained. In the first of these, there are four sections: first, the heading and enumeration; second, the explanation of "that which is the refuge for all" and so forth;
third, the summary and return to what was explained starting from "the three practices" below; and fourth, the reconciliation starting from "in this way" below.
In the initial enumeration of the three dharmas, the first one is designated as the general heading for the following three, which are then listed individually.

However, this scriptural text contains seven phrases, which are grouped into these three [sections]: the first phrase constitutes the "place of refuge"; the next three phrases constitute the "act of taking refuge";
and the final three phrases constitute "non-discrimination. Regarding the commentary on the first phrase, the explanatory text consists of five points, the first of which is the general overview.
The first phrase is explained as that to which the above [preceding section] returns; the second phrase explains its ground, which is the essence of the ground;
the third phrase explains the meaning of "ground" (*bhūmi*); the fourth phrase explains "patience" (*kṣānti*), which is the function of the ground;

and the final phrase concludes the name. These three explanations of the first phrase are thus completed, as can be seen. Next, the explanation of "acting as the basis" (*mūla-bhūta*) explains the subsequent three phrases.
In the eight lines of the commentary, the first two lines provide a general explanation of the meaning of "forming the basis," which can be understood through both the simile and its application.
"If one attains the principle" and below, the remaining three lines of the sutra text are individually analyzed according to the meanings of the four phrases.
"Immeasurable merit" serves as a summary to manifest the efficacy. "The ground has no place for arising" concludes by indicating that each has its own sphere of activity. Next is the explanation.
"Non-discrimination" explains the final three phrases; since these are explained in contrast to the preceding two meanings, one does not discriminate between the two.

The text provides only a brief explanation and the summary of the names, from which it can be understood that there are no three. The following is a general conclusion regarding the identity of name and meaning:
while the essence and function are one, their essence and function are inconceivable; thus, although there are no three, they appear as three. This is to be understood.
Next, the fourth assembly below follows the three dharmas explained in the preceding sutra; these are fully present within this act of donning the robes.
As it is with these two, so it is with the others; therefore, in the previous explanation, each instance was shown to possess all three meanings.
This is precisely because, in this context, the explanation is given according to two dharmas: the former clarifies the capacity to produce, while the latter...
