Otherwise, it would not be possible to fully elucidate that scope, as the text contains the meanings of subject and object, as well as general and specific aspects.
Therefore, regarding the first explanation, it primarily clarifies the wisdom-observation (*prajñā-vipaśyanā*) which assists and completes what preceded; thus, the next two [explanations] follow.

The "Watchman's Summary" explains contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) by means of two aspects; this is because there are these two meanings: the essence is the method, and the characteristic is the characteristic.
Furthermore, since it has already been generally stated that one should contemplate all phenomena as empty, one must distinguish the characteristics of that emptiness.

Because the eighteen [emptinesses] are the most essential, they are used as the basis for this explanation. Since emptiness possesses these eighteen distinctions, it is appropriate [to explain them here].

This is the general and specific classification of this contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). It is thus summarized; one should further examine it in detail. When categorized according to their respective types, there are nine;
when all their characteristics are fully exhausted, there are eighteen. These eighteen are precisely what was indicated in the general heading as "all phenomena" (*sarva-dharma*).
All phenomena are existence, and emptiness is the ultimate non-existence. To speak briefly, these are paired with the single emptiness and collectively termed [the contemplation of] emptiness.

There are those who speak of it in succession because it corresponds to the Middle Way; thus, there is both the infinite and the finite. However, this principle is quiescent and transcendent, being neither existent nor non-existent.
Because it arises from causes and conditions, it is existent; because it has not been heard of since antiquity, one does not know its non-existence, yet it is eternally existent.

Now, in order to cause one to know that it is non-existent yet not non-existent, I shall provide this analysis to cause one to know that it is non-existent yet eternally existent. This is precisely [the purpose].
One should understand that this is the intended meaning of this sutra. Regarding the first section, each of the three categories contains two meanings;

the first two meanings are clearly indicated by the headings of the text, while the second meaning—the wisdom of contemplation—should be further carefully considered. Furthermore, the two [meanings] within the summary are also object and contemplation;
one should reflect upon them. However, although there are three layers of meaning in this summary, they consist of only two, the first two of which are based on...
The two types of fetters refer to the general and the specific; the latter is a "repeated fetter. The three fetters and the three dharma-fetters refer to the contemplation of the three objects;
reflect upon this.

Regarding the statement in the verse that it is "the first line," one should say "one and a half lines," as a half-character has been omitted from the text; otherwise, it would not conform to the metrical requirements of the verse.

One should understand that there are briefly five differences between the verses (*kārikā*) and the prose commentary (*bhāṣya*): namely, their order, their brevity or extensiveness, their opening or closing, their intermingling, and their repetition.
Reflect on this. In the fourth line, one should contrast it with the preceding [lines]; whereas the first three lack compassion, this one does not.
The samatha and vipaśyanā coverings merely manifest alternately. Why is this? As in the previous chapter where entering the room was primary, in this chapter the robe and seat are the first;

such is the proper application of mental activity. The preceding was based on practice and likewise manifested alternately: the first three [chapters] take oneself as the basis for others, so two must be one;
the latter one takes others as the basis, so one must be two. If there were no self, there would be no other, and thus they would not differ from the two.
If one relies on others but lacks [the three qualities] oneself, one does not differ from ordinary beings, and thus it is not a practice of peaceful bliss;

therefore, each and every practice must inherently possess these three. How much more so in this passage, which says: "When I attain Bodhi, I shall lead them by means of supernormal powers and wisdom to cause them to be born within this Dharma.
This is because one attains Bodhi for oneself precisely through the fulfillment of these three dharmas, arising from a mind of compassion and concentration.
Arising through the power of supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi-bala*) and arising from the power of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), if these three powers were absent, how could one attain *bodhi*?
If these three powers were absent, how could one even cause [others] to practice, let alone the subsequent verses which first set forth the text on "reflection" (*cintā*)—

explaining the latter part of the verse by clarifying the two sections on the "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and so forth— and which contain accounts of dreams that explain the causes without doubt.

Regarding the meaning of the *Mārga-varga* (Chapter on the Path), its significance was not understood, and everyone gave rise to doubts and strangeness. Some said that since there was no underlying reason for it, it should not be used;
others said it must be an explanation of subsequent passages that had been misplaced here by error. Now, I say this is not so.

This text is extremely essential, nor is it out of order. Why? For although the *mārga-varga* consists of the numerical categories of the dharmas for practicing the path, [it serves a vital function].
The thirty-seven categories, when grouped together, constitute the fulfillment of the sevenfold course of practice;
this is the correct interpretation of the scriptural passage stating that "after seeking the Way for seven days, one attains the wisdom of all Buddhas.

"Seeking the Way for seven days" means that through the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the sevenfold course is accomplished. "Attaining the wisdom of all Buddhas" refers to the practice of these seven...

Having categorized [the teachings], one immediately attains entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Since all seven categories take contemplative wisdom as their primary focus, they are metaphorically compared to the sun;
otherwise, how could these two phrases be resolved? Therefore, they are of paramount importance.
It is not that there is no sequential order, yet among the seven categories, only two are explicitly explained; this is precisely because explaining these two reveals the remainder.
This is because there are five [reasons]. What are they? Explaining the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) explains the preceding three, the fourth, and the last one;

explaining the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) subsumes the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). These are fully contained within the text, which one may find for oneself upon investigation.

Therefore, I have explained only two [categories], for the meaning of the seven is self-evident. While all schools of the One Teaching explain the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), none of them have yet included what is found herein.
The meaning of this explanation is that since the various scriptures and treatises present different accounts, this interpretation is the most convenient;

therefore, it is clarified here. Within the initial formal explanation of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), there are two main sections. First, regarding the explanation of faith (*śraddhā*), the "Three Jewels" (*triratna*) are the objects of faith.
While there are four [categories] in the original vehicle, one more is added here to complete the set; for now, they shall be explained generally.
Since one must first take this as the foundation prior to practicing cultivation, the initial clarification states that "zǔhuài" (阻壞) is a scribal error;

it should correctly be pronounced *zǔ* (with the phonetic reading *cí lǚ*). This refers to "ruin" or "destruction. Many people do not understand this pronunciation and arbitrarily change it to "zhǔ" (阻), which is incorrect.

The two meanings of "advancing" (*jìn*) and "mindfulness" (*niàn*) are clearly contrasted with each other; "concentration" (*dìng*) refers to the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), all of which are concentration.
This is because of the underlying meaning (*artha*). One should know that here, when the meanings of the Sūtras and Śāstras are compared, one must not seek their sequence based on conventional usage;

the names of these five powers are entirely identical to those of the faculties (*indriya*). However, while the faculties take the sense of "growing" (*utpādana*), the powers take the sense of "capacity" (*samarthya*); since this latter sense is the same as the conventional usage, it is not stated again.
Next, another layer of explanation specifically interprets the preceding meaning in terms of the arousal of the bodhicitta;
since it is stated here that one arouses the mind toward the supreme object, this must specifically pertain to the Mahāyāna.

The term "Tathāgata" used in each instance refers to the arising of these five kinds of practices upon the true suchness (tathatā) of the dharmadhātu; in every case, one must necessarily do so by means of arousing the bodhicitta.
In the main body of this text, only the beginning is stated and the subsequent parts are omitted; those who understand this may seek them out for themselves.

Next, I shall explain the final section on the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). Now, although the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are manifold, sometimes the Eightfold Path is placed first and the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are placed later;
however, here, because we are following the sequential order of the stages, the Eightfold Path is placed last, which should accord with the sacred teaching (*āgama*).

Since the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) explained previously do not differ from the meaning of "constant," they are not explained again; however, the eightfold right path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) is explained.

As for the term "path" (*mārga*), it carries the sense of "cause" as well as the sense of "place of practice. It is that which is relied upon and that which is employed. Regarding the meaning of the term, there are two senses:
the sense of "principle" (*nīti*) and the sense of "benefit" (*artha*). *Śramaṇa* is translated here as "diligent cessation"; it means to diligently cultivate the Path and to cease all afflictions.

This is because the accumulated manifestation of the Way and the removal of what is non-true can be combined to form this name; it is also the name for the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*).

"Cessation" (*śānti*) means tranquility, and it also means exhaustion. To say "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) refers to the exhaustion of all afflictions (*kleśa*) that have been fully present since beginningless time.
Because the fruit (*phala*) encompasses both the partial and the ultimate, there are four [types]. Alternatively, the two characters "accomplishment" may be attributed to the preceding phrase.
For now, let us consider the meaning of "śramaṇa" below; this term applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and the names of the four fruits are likewise to be understood in this way.

Next, we shall explain the meaning of "dream," which consists of three parts. First, regarding the existence or non-existence of dreams: it is first clarified that five types of persons possess them, while the one person who is the Buddha does not.

Furthermore, the reason why the Buddha has no dreams is explained: because he lacks two specific conditions [the *ālayavijñāna* and the *manovijñāna*], which serves as a negative illustration (*paryudāsa*) of what was stated previously.
Regarding these five types of people, because they possess these two factors, there is a sequence from these five matters that leads down to a general clarification of the causes for all dreams.
There are seven matters in total that serve as their causes, which can be understood from the text. If one consults the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are nineteen matters therein concerning dreams.
Furthermore, secular classics such as the *Zhouli* and the works of Liezi likewise clarify six types of dreams (and so forth). Based on this...

Below, there are four further rounds of questions and answers that analyze and resolve doubts; the meanings of the first two rounds have already been presented above and may be sought within the seven matters.
The discussion of the second and third rounds concerns the sleeper: although there are many prior causes for dreaming, if one does not sleep, dreams will not occur.
Therefore, these are discussed again. The first round provides a general discussion on how [dreaming] is common to all.
The latter reason explains a specific doubt to clarify that although they are the same, they are distinct. To speak of "the covering of delusion" (*moha*) refers to the cause of sleep;

when the darkness and obscuration of ignorance (*avidyā*) are forever exhausted without remainder, this is precisely "non-duality. Since it was previously stated that because there is neither doubt nor wisdom, there is no dreaming—and thus no sleep—stating now that there *is* [sleep] appears contradictory. How is this to be reconciled? [Answer: It is answered as follows: ... (as above). This is because the former statement regarding the absence of sleep was made from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), whereas the present statement regarding its existence is made from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the term "sleep" here does not refer to the physical state of lying down with eyes closed, but rather to the mental state of being obscured by the darkness of ignorance. When that darkness is extinguished, one is said to be "awake," even while remaining in a state of meditative equipoise. Thus, the two statements are not in conflict. This is the meaning.
The intention is to demonstrate that he is the same as those in the world. There are two reasons why there are sleeping Buddhas who manifest this sameness with the world:
first, because they wish to initiate present activities; second, because they wish to regulate their physical bodies.
Thus, they externally manifest the appearance of sleep, but it does not exist internally in reality. The meaning clarifies that while the body is the same, the mind is different.
This is because the mind is free from delusion and free from hindrances; this is the meaning elucidated within the Tripiṭaka teachings.
From Chapter Fifteen, "The Emergence from the Earth":

this corresponds to the two capacities, but by following the capacity to respond, one immediately knows there is a capacity to summon; thus, there are again two capacities, each pertaining to a person.

That which can respond to people is called the work of a Bodhisattva; that which can summon people is the work of a Buddha. Regarding the sound of speech, within the capacity to respond, one merely knows through the phenomenon that there is a person.
Furthermore, each of these two capacities has three aspects. Within the capacity to summon, the three refer to the person, the phenomenon, and the intention.

In the title, none of these are present; within the text, two of the intentions are entirely hidden. Within the capacity to respond, the three refer to the person... [text ends]... the phenomenon, and the intention.
In terms of the meaning, these three [passages] all manifest in the text; based on this, they respond to the three [aspects of] manifestation, concealment, and summoning.

Furthermore, although both chapters contain the text regarding the emergence of the assembly, the titles differ: the former mentions "seeing" (*darśana*) but not "emergence," while the latter mentions "emergence" (*utsarjana*) but not "seeing.
Moreover, whereas the former contains both manifest and secret aspects, this chapter exclusively manifests [the secret], and it emerges from within the former itself.
This chapter is so named because it summons and commands this teacher, and because it also concerns that which is called the Dharma (and so forth). The titles of the various chapters differ;
this particular chapter is named after the person and the event. In full, it should be called "The Chapter on the Bodhisattvas Emerging from the Earth.
"Bodhisattvas" refers to the persons; "emerging from the earth" refers to the event. Within this chapter, they are termed "the bodhisattvas emerging from the earth."

Because it is appropriate to name this person after these matters, it is stated thus. Although the naming is derived briefly from the phenomena, the meaning of the "three" is already manifest within it;

therefore, there is no need for further elaboration. Furthermore, since this chapter clarifies the "summoner" and the "respondent," the title is taken directly from the "respondent," which likewise naturally reveals the presence of the "summoner. Moreover, the Sūtra takes [the title] directly from...
To take "Able to Respond" (*nengfu*) as the name and interpret the meaning directly from its capacity to summon is not merely an excellent commentary on the title of the sutra;
it is also a marvelous exposition. Being concise yet comprehensive, this is truly what is meant by [an ideal commentary].

Since both of these meanings are present in the text of the commentary, without grasping this intent, the text of the sutra and the commentary will not be easily understood. In the commentary’s explanation of the name, there are two aspects.

In the first section of the separate explanation regarding the definition of the title, there are further two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the summary. The first part contains four meanings:

first, clarifying the response of teacher and disciple to the call; second, extensively clarifying the benefits for the three periods of time; third, refuting the near to reveal the far; and fourth, opening up the near to reveal the far.
These four meanings combined constitute the title, which is precisely the intent of the Fourfold Accommodation (catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastu); therefore, it is said thus.

Furthermore, these four meanings do not transcend the categories of the general and the specific, which consist of three layers. In each case, the first serves as the general and the latter three as the specific.
"General" refers to the overall category that encompasses the latter three; although they are called "specific," the first remains the general.

As for the initial general meaning, it refers to being named simply by coming in response to the teacher's summons. The "specific" refers to the fact that there are three distinct intentions in responding to the summons. From this combination of the general and the specific...
This is considered to be the name. Furthermore, the first [part] directly explains the name as a whole; the next three [parts] specifically clarify its meaning.

From this, the general and specific meanings and intents are combined to form the name. Moreover, the first [part] directly clarifies that he came by imperial command, without yet mentioning the intent of the "original" (hon) and "traces" (ji);
the subsequent three all specifically discuss the intent of the original and traces. From this, the general and specific [elements] are combined to constitute the name.
This is because the names are formed by combining the meanings of these three aspects—both general and specific—and thus it is said as such.
Without grasping these three points, the text is difficult to interpret.
Within the first meaning, there are five phrases: the first four correctly explain the name in terms of responding to the summons of life, while the last one provides the conclusion.
The establishment of the title [of this treatise] proceeds from the first two lines of the opening verse. The first two lines generally cite worldly teachers and disciples as a point of analogy;

the subsequent two lines properly apply this analogy to reveal the specific meaning herein. Within the first pair of lines, the first line clarifies the teacher and the second line clarifies the disciple.

The first line originates from Confucian sources; thus, the *Lixue ji* (Record of Rites) states: "Only when the teacher is revered does the Way become honored; only when the Way is honored... [and so forth].
Later, when the people came to know how to revere learning, Zheng Xuan’s commentary explained that "yan" (嚴) means "reverent respect" (*jing-jin*).
This implies that a student must first maintain reverent respect toward their teacher, and only then will they honor the Way; in this way, everyone comes to revere learning.
Although the words here are borrowed from that context, the intended meaning is different. Why? Because within this context, there are generally three meanings.
This refers to the teacher, the Way, and virtue. The text says "teacher" to clarify that he is the instructor; "venerable" to clarify that the teacher’s virtue is complete;

and "honored in the Way" to clarify that the teacher’s realization of the Way is supreme. That the teacher can act as a craftsman to perfect those who seek liberation—this is what is meant by "venerable," signifying that the teacher’s virtue is perfectly good and free from all blemishes; and "Way," signifying that the teacher’s Way is all-pervasive. This pertains to the mundane world.

"Regarding 'the ultimate of the teacher' (師之極也): the phrase 'exhausting the resources' (資者鞠窮盡也) means to fully utilize one's person (躬身). 'Respectfully' (祗) means reverence; 'to receive and follow' (奉承順也) means to comply with and uphold [the teacher's will].

Even if one is a teacher, if their moral virtue (道德) is not ultimate and their dignity is not profound, the disciple (資) will be unable to exhaust their physical form and mind to reverently receive and follow them.
Since these three meanings are complete, one exhausts both body and mind to receive and follow; therefore, it is said thus. These two [points] are the correct [interpretation]."

"To go together with the kind" refers to the second of the two [sections below]. Furthermore, if even the worldly masters and disciples are like this, how much more so for the Buddha, whose three virtues are perfected to the ultimate degree?
Even when told to go at the cost of one's life, they do not fail to leap forward in haste; thus it is said, "At a single command of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
The first phrase corresponds to the three meanings of the preceding section, while the second phrase corresponds to the sentence immediately above. As for "a single command," it means "one."
The phrase "going forth with the summons" (*onmyō*) refers to a single line, a single verse, or a single invocation used to summon [the spirits] from the four directions;

these are all collectively considered one. Regarding the "four directions," the sutra states that the earth in the four directions quakes and splits, and [the beings] all emerge from within, appearing on the four sides directly facing the place where the Tathāgata sits. "Concluding" (*ketsu*) means to respond to this summons by attending upon the Master.

It is said "coming for the sake of the Dharma" (yi) because they have come for that purpose; one should know that within this there is a reciprocal meaning, as the former does not mention "summoning" (ming) and the latter does not mention "virtue and morality" (daode).

Next, regarding the three distinct meanings below: the previous section only mentioned gathering to attend to the teacher's summons for the sake of sustenance, yet it was not known who the teacher was.
What is the intent behind this invocation? To clarify it now, there are three essential points, all of which emerge from the preceding unity.

First is the general [intention], followed by three specific ones. Furthermore, within the first point there are seven phrases: the first six correctly clarify the Buddha’s intent in invoking [the assembly], and the last one concludes by explaining how the name is obtained.
Within the first of these, the initial two phrases clarify the Buddha’s fundamental and manifested traces (*honji-suijaku*) of transformation.
The next two lines clarify the general object of the benefit: that which was not previously taught and was unknown to beings lacks profound benefit.

The following two lines indicate that by causing them to know [it], they obtain wondrous benefit; therefore, it is summoned as the "Three Times," which refers to the manifestation of transformation through both the fundamental and the trace aspects.
"Wisdom" (hui) means bestowing grace upon all things, which is to say compassion and benefit. "Jiangjie" (疆界) means boundaries.
This clarifies that the benefits bestowed are manifold. The single moon is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s transformative path throughout the three periods of time.
The myriad reflections are a metaphor for the boundless nature of his wisdom and benefit; the benefits conferred are exceedingly great. "Who could fathom this?

means that the benefits bestowed upon beings in both worlds cannot be fully known. It is precisely so that they may know [the Buddha] and thereby obtain these benefits that he calls out to them; therefore, it is said, "He summons."

"Passing away and so forth" means that [the Buddha] summons those who have benefited [him] in the past, manifests his presence in the present, and causes those in the future to likewise obtain benefit.
Thus, "propagating the sutra" refers to the sublime Dharma of the two gates of circulation.

This is fully explained as it pertains to the *Ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra* (Exertion of Supernatural Power) and the *Parīndanā* (Entrustment) chapters. As for the final conclusion, the preceding text was still brief, mentioning only the intent behind the Buddha’s summons.
It is not that the mind of those who go is not correct; rather, it should further be said that the Bodhisattvas come because of the meaning of this Buddha’s summons.
It is called "going in response to the summons" (shōfu) precisely because they come from this point in response to the call; therefore, it is so named.

Regarding the next section on "Intention," the text also consists of seven phrases: the first six correctly clarify the Buddha’s intention in summoning [the assembly], while the final one concludes by establishing the title.
Within the first part, there are initially two phrases clarifying that the Buddha’s cultivated virtues have both a fundamental source and a manifest trace;

next, there are two phrases clarifying that [these virtues] are entirely unknown and cannot be eliminated by others, as they remove the obstruction of ultimate darkness; finally, there are two phrases correctly explaining that [the Buddha] acts specifically to remove the general, ultimate darkness.

Therefore, regarding the metaphors used for the beginning and middle of the invocation, some are explained by means of phenomena and principle, while others are explained through both general and specific senses. Here, however, the primary intent is to clarify the relationship between the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku).

To explain the cultivation of the manifested, one must first discuss the inherent non-existence of the fundamental. Now, since the nature-merit (*prakṛti-guṇa*) is like space, how could there be "early" or "late"?

"Early" refers to the fundamental, which has been accomplished for a long time; "late" refers to the manifested, which is accomplished more recently. The nature is precisely the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), which is without [temporal distinction].
Regarding the two aspects, no one debates whether they are distant or near; yet there are not two [aspects] that do not arise from causes and conditions. Thus it is said that "there are two," namely:
that which is cultivation while being the very nature (*svabhāva*), and that which is self-originated or other-originated. Because it has been accomplished over a long duration, it is called "early";

because the objects [of practice] are not fixed, there is the "near" trace. The previous explanation is thus: within this text, since these meanings also exist, the preceding and succeeding sections can mutually clarify one another.

Next, I shall clarify that the reason beings do not know [the truth] is because the preceding sutra did not yet state that beings are entirely ignorant of the existence of both the provisional (迹) and the real (本).

It is precisely because this was not stated that they cling to the provisional as being real, and thus remain entirely ignorant. Furthermore, their prior clinging to the provisional means they were entirely ignorant of both the provisional and the real.
The cause for this clinging is that [the truth] had never been explained until now; it is due to this clinging that [they fail to understand].
This is because they cannot destroy the obstruction of extreme darkness. It is precisely for the sake of destroying this that they are summoned and also come. To summarize:
these bodhisattvas come in response to the Buddha’s intention in summoning them; they are so named because they arrive from this [summons]. Therefore, it is said thus.

Regarding the final meaning, the text consists of only five phrases: the first four summon the mind, and the last one concludes the name. Within the first [section], the first two phrases clarify the fundamental and manifested traces (*honjaku*) of the teacher and disciple.
The first phrase clarifies that the Teacher manifested his trace by attaining realization at the site of *Jikkyō* (the Place of Quiescence); this is the place where he first attained the Way.

The old term was "Jikkyō Dōjō" (Place of the Path of Quiescent Extinction), while the new term is "Bodaijō" (Bodhi-maṇḍala). Though the words differ, the meaning is the same. The metaphor of the "younger father" refers to the Buddha.

The meaning of the "recently accomplished" *Sukhāvatī* (Jìguāng) can be understood as signifying the place where the fundamental [reality] is accomplished, because the various bodhisattvas dwell in the lower space.
The metaphor of the "old man" emerging refers to a multitude whose status is so exalted that they do not recognize him.
This analogy of the old and the young is fully contained in the subsequent text; this clarifies that while the Tathāgata manifests traces, the bodhisattvas exist as such from the fundamental [state].
The manifestation of differences is precisely intended to reveal the original ground by means of the power of the medicine.

As in the previous example of the inversion between old and young, where different beings were all unaware and incapable of reaching the wondrous Way, it is now revealed that the present is itself the wondrous essence;

therefore, it is said thus. For those of meager virtue and heavy defilement who do not delight in hearing of the long-established [Buddhahood], the Tathāgata provides this as a prescription for the sick.

The medicine of the traces (*jì*) also manifests as having been newly attained; therefore, for those whose fathers—representing Bodhisattvas with slight defilements and obscurations—delight in hearing teachings on the long-distant path, they take the medicine of "revealing the origin to manifest the fundamental" (*fā jì xiǎn běn*). Because they occupy a position of actual reality, the sons—representing Buddhas—are old.

By means of this, the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*) is opened regarding the Buddha, while the aspect of ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*) is shown regarding the Bodhisattva. These aspects manifest together to achieve a single unity.
This ensures that all may come to know that it is not a matter of being old or young; this clarifies the benefit of the revelation and manifestation in the Root Gate (*mūla-mukha*).
That is to say, it causes all beings to attain the opening, showing, awakening to, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*).

By briefly citing the single term "knowing," the four types of knowledge and vision are comprehensively encompassed. While the previous Trace Gate merely caused them to enter [the path], this Root Gate causes them to [attain] it here.

The fourth is the ultimate advancement; it is also for this purpose that they are summoned. "Assembling" (*saṃnipatita*) clarifies that the various bodhisattvas, responding to this intent of the summons, hasten and arrive in alarm. It is named after this meaning of responding to the command; therefore, it is so called.
Because this name is established based on these four meanings in total, it is termed "etcetera" (*ādi*). The passage beginning with "As for the text below... is the next summary.
The "Connection" (*jieti*) explains the source from which [the following] proceeds. By what causes and conditions does this inquiry arise? It arises from the four *siddhāntas* (purposes).
Since the essentials of cause and effect do not exceed these four, they are used as the explanation. Previously, it was stated directly that there is "one life";

how is it known that it must necessarily possess all four? Since it was stated that it is "for the sake of enabling beings to attain the ultimate Buddha[-nature]," [it follows that the four are complete].
One must know that it is impossible to do so with fewer than four; therefore, they must necessarily be four. The meanings of these four preceding items appear easy yet are difficult;

at present, I have not yet been able to fully prepare them, so you should examine them in detail yourself. A small portion of this section follows from the original text and does not require a separate version.

It may be sought after the "Chapter on Merit" (Gongde pin). From here below, the teaching, the origin and manifestation (benji), and the gates of contemplation (guanmen) are to be considered and extracted.
The following is the second section, which explains and resolves the text. Regarding the initial statement that marks the chapter door, saying "this is a major section" and so forth:

one might ask, "Since there was no such categorization previously, why is this statement present now? We reply that the intent here is indeed profound and far-reaching, yet it is explained as follows:

All [previous commentators] have considered this to be superficial and have remained silent; now, being unable to restrain myself, I shall briefly explain it. Why is this? The Sūtra contains both general and specific meanings.
When it speaks of the two gates of the fundamental and the trace, this meaning is general. If it speaks of "opening up the provisional to reveal the real," this meaning is specific.
"General" means it applies universally to both the teacher and the disciple, as well as to the capacity and the object; "specific" refers to...
The former [teaching] is limited to the subject who transforms, failing to penetrate the objective resources being transformed;

furthermore, it represents a horizontal-vertical distinction, as the Trace Gate (Jikimon) discusses the revelation [of the Buddha-nature] by way of the ten realms, which is horizontal, whereas the Origin Gate (Honmon) discusses the revelation of the three periods of time solely in terms of the Buddha, which is vertical.
Since the former has already concluded its discussion of the distinct [teaching] and the horizontal revelation, we shall now proceed to discuss the universal [teaching] and the vertical [revelation].
In this treatise, I have addressed the essential meanings directly; being concise yet praising [the subject], commentators generally pay no heed to it.

As for the "Master’s School," this already clarifies that the preceding [section] reveals the disciples’ original and manifested traces—such as those of Śrīmitra, Kumārajīva, and others at the end of the third century.
Yet, even these do not clarify that the Master and his disciples still possess distant traces; how much less could there be a Master who lacks a long-standing origin?

Regarding what is called the "proximate trace," this refers merely to a single lifetime. However, while the disciples manifest their origin by still encompassing the causal stage, the Master’s origin is directed solely toward the ultimate fruit;
therefore, it is further described as the "distant origin" of the Buddha-ground. This fundamental origin, as illustrated by the subsequent points, is even more vast than these numbers.
All the essential subtleties of this sutra—whether horizontal or vertical, general or specific—are fully contained within these two phrases, both of which are [treated] with...
It is regrettable that there is not a single word of appreciation for this ordinary matter; alas, alas!

It may be said that when people speak of their inner thoughts with such breathless intensity, yet others treat them as if they were mere trifles, it is truly lamentable. This is roughly how it stands. Having received your letter, you ought to reflect further upon it.

What follows below is the second section, which provides an exegesis of the text. First, regarding the indication of the chapter headings, the phrase "the great sections," etc., refers to what preceded.
In the initial sectioning of the text, this title did not exist, yet its inclusion here—does this not indicate a difference?

One must not fail to understand that what is intended now is simply to clarify the preceding meaning through a different name. In the second part of the previous sectioning, it was divided according to two gates, stating:
"The first fourteen chapters concern the Trace Gate (*jìmén*) in its revelation of the provisional to manifest the real; from this present chapter onward..."

The fourteen chapters, based on the Original Gate (*honmon*), reveal the provisional to manifest the real (*kaiken*). Now, this chapter specifically re-establishes this thematic framework and is thus given this title.

Although the underlying intent is no different, when speaking of their distinct expressions, it is appropriate that they be harmonized. Previously, the commentaries did not state that there was any point where the principle remained unclarified;
yet, I shall now venture to speak of it. Why? Because when we speak of "Original" (*hon*) and "Trace" (*saku*), both of these belong to the capacity of the transformer (*nōke*).

This Sage does not involve himself with other persons. As for the statement regarding "opening the provisional to reveal the real," this refers to the distinction between the Trace Gate (*jìmén*), which is considered from the perspective of the object, and the Origin Gate (*běnmén*), which is considered from the perspective of the subject. To say it is "from the perspective of the object" means the persons being transformed, namely the three vehicles and the nine realms.
The text says, "all those seeking the three vehicles," and "desiring to cause all multitudes [to attain enlightenment]"—this is precisely for their sake.
These individuals who reveal [the truth] are precisely those disciples to be transformed; that is to say, they are universally all sentient beings.
Therefore, the text says: "The sentient beings therein are all my children. This is the meaning revealed in the Trace Gate (*jimon*).

Regarding what is called the "Opening and Revealing" from the perspective of the Fundamental Gate (*honmon*), this refers to the one who performs the transformation—that is, the Master; the Master is the Buddha.

Furthermore, according to the previous agreement, those to be transformed may be either universal or limited. Disciples are limited, whereas sentient beings are universal. Since they are limited [in the case of disciples], it is appropriate that they be universal;

thus, this contains two meanings. Now, this case is also like that: while the term "Teacher" (śāstṛ) remains universal, we further cite the Buddha specifically to clarify his person; therefore, both terms are used.
Regarding the fundamental [truth], when one speaks of "opening up the provisional to reveal the real," this refers to the trace and the fundamental.
However, because the provisional and the real are fundamentally that which has been self-attained since time immemorial, they constitute the "real trace.

That which is manifested for the sake of sentient beings throughout the three periods of past, present, and future—from the intermediate period after that until today—is the provisional. Although the names "provisional" and "real" are the same in these two gates, their significance and essence do not differ;
in brief, they simply differ in being horizontal and vertical. You should contemplate this well. Now, as for this form...
The two meanings within the preceding section are why he is called both "Teacher" and "Buddha. To speak thus is to manifest their respective excellences;
if it were not so, the essential points would differ, and one could only trust in the author’s ingenuity. This meaning is profound and remote, difficult to comprehend in moments of haste;
one can only look up to it in reverence. For now, this is a brief summary; one should contemplate it well, as it has been presented with particular care.
Chapter Sixteen: On the Lifespan (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*).
In order to explain this title, one must first understand the reason for its designation as well as the distinction between its general and specific meanings;
only then can one discern the correctness or error of ancient and modern interpretations. Why is this? This chapter is named after both the person and the dharma: the Tathāgata...
The lifespan of this person and this Dharma are explained extensively in this chapter; because it takes this wondrous person and Dharma as its title, it is described in such a way.
Regarding the "general and specific" (tongbie): while the name and meaning are general, the intent is specific. Why?

Because names and meanings such as these exist identically in both the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, they are therefore general. However, [this text] clarifies only the future and does not clarify...
The meaning of the past *honji-suijaku* (original and manifested) has now been correctly clarified through the meaning of the *honji-suijaku* across the three periods of time;

therefore, while this is termed "universal," its underlying intent is eternally distinct. This gate is said to be most difficult to comprehend because, when observing the interpretations of the ancients and the present day through these two meanings, they have only grasped the universal sense and entirely failed to distinguish the specific. How can such [interpretations] be worthy of praise or manifestation?
How marvelous is this commentary! It is likewise divided into two parts. First, the titles; within the first [of these], there may also be two divisions, namely the general and the specific.

Within the initial explanation of the names, there are four sections: first, recounting divergent interpretations by predecessors; next, distinguishing and establishing the meanings of those differences. Regarding the second [section]: "The Heron."

From the section on "The Oyster" (*Pāṅ*) downward, three pairs of divergent meanings are presented briefly to indicate the core tenets; from the "Chapter on Explaining the Meaning" (*Shìpǐn*) downward, four sections provide a formal and extensive explanation.
Now, these four [sections] constitute the ultimate core of the Great Matter (*mahā-vastu*) and its causal conditions (*nidāna*), and are not merely incidental.

Since this sutra possesses two kinds of wondrousness, one must first understand what is incorrect before clarifying what is correct; therefore, the divergences are first distinguished. Although they are recounted, it was previously unknown which [was the true teaching].

Because they differ from one another, the following section distinguishes their establishment. Since one must know what is correct once one has understood what is incorrect, yet this cannot be revealed all at once, it is therefore stated briefly.
Furthermore, because the underlying principle is not yet exhaustive, it must be explained extensively; thus, there are these four chapters. Reflect upon them:
within each of these four, there are two meanings, and within the first [chapter], there are two: the general heading and the specific exposition.
Regarding the second point within the third section, there are two parts: first, a general summary that definitively establishes the two distinct meanings of priority and posteriority;

and second, a specific refutation of the latter’s adherence to the views of identity and difference. Within these three [subsections], the first provides a concise demonstration of the four meanings—both partial and complete—in contrast to the two preceding schools.

Next, it sets forth a critical analysis of the subsequent intent. Furthermore, regarding the second part within the fourth meaning, there are two sections: first, the direct explanation; and second, the analytical discussion.
Contemplate and reflect deeply upon the intent of the "Chapter on Revealing the Original through the Trace.

First, regarding the presentation of divergent interpretations (*yìjiě*), this clarifies that their understanding of the scripture’s purport is not yet complete and does not accord with one's own view; thus they are termed "divergent interpretations.

Furthermore, because their essential meanings are identical, these are specifically cited here. The first, third, and fifth [versions] were translated by the same person who personally received them from Master Kumārajīva;
the second was translated by someone in Xiliang together with Dharmakṣema, the translator of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;
and the commentator is Liu Qiu, a high-minded scholar of the Southern Qi dynasty, though they are not arranged in chronological order.
Some say that these are not necessarily the correct sequence and are merely for the sake of convenience; why must there be a fixed order?

Others say that because the meaning of "arising" (birth) is somewhat broader, it is placed later. Now, I maintain that the first three [sections] are all composed as a preface to this sutra, as clarified in the preface itself.

The sequence of that preface is fully recorded in Sengyou’s *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through the Ages) of the Liang dynasty; however, this is merely a general discussion of the meaning of the "Root Chapter" (Honmon).
The phrase "the commentary on the title of the 'Non-Orthodox Exposition' chapter" refers precisely to the commentary within the main exposition that explains the meaning of this chapter's title;

The "three meanings" refer to the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the three lifespans (*trāyuṣa*). Regarding these three bodies and three lifespans, each possesses four permutations—namely, limited, unlimited, and so forth—which must be distinguished.

Fourth, one must clarify the distinction between the cultivated (*bhāvanā*) and the innate (*prakṛti*); although the term "cultivated and innate" appears to be general in its application to the preceding three meanings, here it specifically clarifies the merit of cultivation.

Although there are four [aspects], the present intention lies precisely in the original four from long ago. Otherwise, these would merely represent the general meaning found across various sutras rather than the specific intent of this section;
thus, it can be clearly understood that the reasons for these five [aspects] have come forth (and so on). Since this chapter contains these five meanings, they must be explained.
Therefore, the current text provides a formal explanation that fully clarifies these five, as was previously described.
The explanations provided by the five schools all lack these five meanings; how could they not be entirely contrary to the intent of the sūtra?
This is precisely why the concluding rebuke states: "These various masters are not fit to be teachers. This is for this very reason.
If those who study this do not understand this meaning, they will be unable to achieve a comprehensive understanding, let alone those others. This section of the commentary should [be placed] here.

The phrase "because the entire body, as well as its numerical measure, are both numbers" serves to clarify the meaning of the lifespan.
If the body were either singular or plural, the lifespan would likewise be either long or short; however, because the body is neither singular nor plural, the lifespan is neither long nor short.
Regarding this specific statement, it must also be investigated and explained why it is not a number: for "long," "short," "near," and "far" are all quantitative measures.
This is because they are things that arise from conditions; it is not that they are permanent. This clearly explains that they are not [permanent].

As for the statement "they are not different," this clarifies that whether one or many, they are all distinct things, yet the reality conforms to their number. Reality is beyond number; being non-different means it is neither one nor many.
Samantabhadra, these two points also explain why his merit has long been perfected and yet he remains within the causal stage—this is because he is eternally as such.
The "position of meaning" (*artha-sthāna*) precisely signifies that while it is accomplished, it is not accomplished; while there is coming, there is no coming;

and while it has been extinguished for a long time, it manifests again—this precisely signifies that while it is extinguished, it is not extinguished. Together, these establish the two preceding meanings. This chapter clarifies the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*;

The reason the lifespan is long is that although the Many-Treasures Stupa had been extinguished for a long time, it appeared once more;

Next, regarding the explanation of "the Teacher" (śāstṛ): this is also a general discussion on the meaning of "longevity" within the sequence [of the text], rather than a definitive interpretation of the title of the chapter.
That passage is extensive; here, I shall briefly summarize it. The text consists of four phrases:

the first two directly establish the essential meaning, while the latter two cite two points to demonstrate its fulfillment. The first term, "clarifying" (ming), refers to this Present Teaching (mūla-parivarta).

The essential point clarified here is precisely as follows: the two meanings that follow are integrated. "Dharmakāya" is mentioned generally; "True and Transformation" clarify the specific distinction;

"Whether existing or perishing, the principle is one" clarifies the lifespan (*āyus-pramāṇa*). Below, the cited text establishes the presence of Prabhūtaratna.
The manifestation of the marks of appearance within this very center is not extinction, yet it is extinction; by means of this non-extinction that is extinction, it is eternally present.

This explains that the true transformation mentioned above is no different [from this]. What is the state of this eternal presence? It is because its lifespan is clarified as being equal to the great void;
this is precisely what the Sūtra calls "permanently abiding and non-extinguished. This refers to the lifespan of the Buddha-body in this Root Chapter.

Regarding the essential meaning of the *Māna* (Measurement), if one observes the Master’s intention, it is a general discussion within the introductory section concerning the essential meaning of the "Root Chapter" (*Honmon*), rather than a formal commentary on the title of this specific chapter.
Although the text generally discusses the beginning and end of the entire work, its primary intent lies in clarifying the essentials of the Root Chapter.
That introductory text is extensive; here too, I shall briefly extract its essentials. The text consists of five phrases.
The first two lines generally indicate the essential meaning of the two gates; the next two lines specifically explain the final phrase of the second [section] above;

therefore, the subsequent two lines specifically explain the meaning of that conclusion, and finally, they are summarized to return to the fundamental essence. First.

The essential summary is not merely for its own sake.

It is precisely to clarify that the Dharma-body is not a life-span, yet is the life-span, and is neither measurable nor immeasurable.
The phrase "as for the measure" (*pramāṇa*) refers to the explicit teaching regarding the lifespan of the *dharmakāya* and so forth; this is the meaning of the intent behind such a statement.

The first sentence cites a prerequisite to initiate the subsequent formal explanation. That is to say, this principle precisely clarifies that the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* is neither form nor substance, and is not encompassed by the calculation of lifespan.
What is the underlying intention? It is precisely that which has already been integrated [into understanding] in the preceding section.

Furthermore, longevity depends upon the body; therefore, why would the body not be that which manifests through response? Thus, he explains it by resolving the matter of responsive manifestation.

This refers to ordinary people of the mundane world who, upon hearing the sūtra, give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and immediately abide in this stage, without before or after—just as in the meaning of *śraddhā-vimukti* (liberation through faith). This is because they are free from the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*).
Because of this cause, there is no result in the form of the wheel of suffering within the three realms.

If one were to say that it is only at this stage that one can generate the mind [of awakening] and enter the ten stages as a long-term distinction, this would not accord with those various sutras and is not the intended meaning here. Next, regarding the attainment of *kṣānti* (patience) as the tenth stage:

realizing the essence of the Middle Way, which is neither arising nor ceasing, is called "anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti" (the patience of the non-arising of phenomena). As for the term "generating the mind," this...
The manifestation of this true essence is called "non-orientation"; the absence of seeking toward external objects is called "uttering words. Regarding "one and all":
within the ten [categories], the first itself possesses ten meanings, and since even the final stage likewise contains them all, it is called "one and all.
To speak in essential terms, these are the three bodies and three virtues. When speaking of "one body," it refers to the True Body (dharmakāya), which is immeasurable.
"The body" refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body); "pure and so forth" explains the purity of the two aforementioned bodies; "excellent body" refers to the aforementioned single body;

and "responding to all" refers to the aforementioned infinite body. If one were to explain the correspondence between the seventh, eighth, ninth, and third stages and the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) according to the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Renwang jing), it would be a matter of distinct, sequential stages rather than this perfect and subtle [teaching]. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is cited as proof to establish the sequence.

Second, regarding the logical necessity of the progression toward the [next] stage: although the scriptural text for the four stages below is abbreviated, their meaning cannot be absent even for a moment;

therefore, they are set forth in full. However, while the total number of stages from beginning to end across the sūtras and śāstras is fifty-two, because this discussion concerns the beginning and end of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), there are fifty-one, corresponding to the number and meaning of the preceding counterparts.
If faith is like a tally and its seal, how could one say it is otherwise?

Commentators of past and present have failed to contemplate the fundamental purport [of the teaching]; instead, they have jumbled together names and definitions from various treatises to explain this text.

Those who do not understand believe this deeply, while those who do understand know it to be incorrect. One must reflect upon this again and again with a subtle mind. Now, as for the preceding passage:

Furthermore, because it speaks of the truth, it says "forty"; because this penetrates the subtle, it says "fifty-one. At the end of the preceding section, the conclusion generally clarifies that rejoicing is indeed universal;
if one does not understand this interpretation, how can one grasp the essential core of the doctrine? Some say:

other sutras still possess the "subtle totality" (*miaozong*) within the very seat [of realization], whereas in this sutra, the two gates of essence and function are exquisitely transcendent; therefore, what is nurtured therein must surely be so.
Why is it that there are those who meet the ultimate source of the school yet rely solely on causes? Briefly, there are two meanings.

First, they are the most difficult [to save], for they are all those who have opened up and shattered the biased provisional teachings of ordinary and small-vehicle practitioners, enabling them to enter together into the stage of the perfect sage. This is because other sutras are mostly intended for those already adjacent to the ultimate.
As a sutra says: "There was a stainless great being who, hearing the Dharma on his very seat, reached the source of the Dharma-nature throughout the ten directions."
To become a Buddha is precisely the proof of this; as these two [texts] are the most concise of the fundamental scriptures, they are described thus for the time being.

If one were to rely on the extensive and complete fundamental texts, there would certainly be the benefit of reaching the ultimate. One must not cling exclusively to the concise version while neglecting the extensive fundamental text;
one should be careful and thorough in this regard. Furthermore, there are other meanings which will be explained in the following order.

Next, the following is the third section on distinguishing and clarifying. Within this, first there is the distinction from the previous two [positions], which concerns the difference between the two meanings of "increase" and "decrease" in the formal treatise.
The term "both" (*bing*) means "not as [stated]," implying they are not identical. What faults do these two schools have? Briefly stated, each has a fault:

first, [the first school] exclusively relies on the meaning of arising from two [causes] to establish their difference; second, [the second school] dogmatically adheres to the two texts to establish their distinctness.
Not knowing their mutual interpenetration results in three deficiencies in total; that is, to the two aforementioned [deficiencies], one further adds the deficiency of "shallow and deep.

Since the former has already been refuted, we now clarify only the two deficiencies. These are explained solely in reference to what follows below, as they differ from the meaning of the preceding two.
How do they differ? Upon examination, it is precisely because of two meanings that they are explained in the sequence presented.

Within this, regarding the dharma that serves as the analogy and the dharma to which it is applied, if one considers them in terms of wisdom (*jñāna*), there is both abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and increase;

if one considers them in terms of augmentation (*vṛddhi*), there is both decrease (*hāni*) and increase. Thus, these two texts possess both meanings and cannot be definitively adjudicated, because the sūtra author has explained them interchangeably. Second, if one speaks only of wisdom and abandonment, both are pervasive throughout cause and fruit;

however, if they are distinguished separately, the sense of their pervasiveness is lost. One must not rigidly insist on such distinctions. For this reason, this case is not the same as that [previous] one.
The second explanation follows the analogy of the moon’s phases, through which the wisdom (*jñāna*) and severance (*prahāṇa*) can be understood.

By summarizing and correlating the body of the moon below with the parable to reveal the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), one knows that although the benefits are vast, they do not transcend these three virtues;

these are also the three bodies (*tri-kāya*), and even extend to the ten kinds of triads as clarified in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). To state it briefly, they are simply the two types of three virtues: the semblance [virtues] and the true [virtues].
As for why the "benefit" (*anuśaṃsa*) is not explained, the meaning of the preceding question and answer may also be applied here to resolve this.
Alternatively, it may be that what follows below constitutes a fourth further explanation of the text; yet, in the subsequent essential passage, there appears to be a lapse in the phrasing.

Because the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) is without fixed direction, it is said that words cannot exhaust its meaning. The Buddha’s statement, "I do not understand my own meaning," refers to what was previously explained:

the four secret utterances are near in meaning yet distant in expression. Because there is no [fixed] truth (in contrast to the one), it is called "non-existent. That is to say, the capacity is neither non-existent nor not non-existent; thus, among the four propositions, there is nothing that is not non-existent. This absence of direction within the four propositions is precisely this.
From the section on "Supernatural Power" (*ṛddhi-bala*) downward, eight chapters clarify the entrustment and circulation; according to this, these constitute eight chapters.

Since both serve the purpose of entrustment (*parindanā*), one knows that there are both general and specific types of entrustment. "General" refers to the fact that all eight chapters may collectively be termed "entrustment";

"specific" refers to the fact that it applies only to the single chapter on Entrustment. Because the Sūtra contains these two meanings, the Commentary follows the intent of the Sūtra by dividing it into two sections.
Having finished hearing the three preceding chapters on the same [truth], as well as the original revelation and manifestation which establish the essence, what follows below is...
The eleven chapters and a half from [the "Expedient Means" chapter] onward represent the circulation of the teaching arising from its essence.

The differences in the repetition between the preceding and succeeding sections may be understood by analogy with the Trace Gate (*jimon*). Furthermore, within the section on differentiation, the four grades of faith during the present age, the five grades after the extinction of the Buddha, as well as the "Merit of Rejoicing" and the "Merit of the Dharma Master" chapters, are an expansion upon the "Dharma Master" chapter of the previous [trace gate]. Within the section on "Never-Disparaging," the disparagement...
The two chapters on "Faith" correspond to those who disparage [the Dharma] in the "Dharmabhāṇaka" chapter above; those who have faith correspond to Devadatta in the "Devadatta" chapter above.
The "Entrustment" (Śakti-parīndanā) corresponds to the "Parīndanā" chapter above. The six chapters beginning with "Bhaiṣajyarāja" correspond to the "Sukhavihāra" (Peaceful Practice) chapter above.
The "Stūpa of the Seven Jewels," "Past Lives of Devadatta," and "Mañjuśrī" [chapters] [correspond to the same].
The current "Chapter on the Dharma-Preacher Holding [the Teaching]" brings peace and happiness to the future; the three periods of the Fundamental Gate are explained accordingly.
Alternatively, the six chapters from "Bhaiṣajyarāja" onwards arise from the essence to manifest function; this is also analogous to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Bhaiṣajyarāja is the sincere teacher, while Gadgadasvara and Avalokiteśvara, or the assembly [of bodhisattvas], cause the teaching to circulate and flourish through these individuals. Both internally and externally, they protect the Dharma. Universally...
The "Worthy One" (Bhadra) penetrates the dharmas of former sages, such that both internal and external dharmas are fully circulated.

According to the intent of the two chapters of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Gandavyūha*) is the essence (*tattva*), while the "Manifestation of the Tathāgata" (*Tathāgatotpatti-sambhava*) is the arising of function (*vṛtti*). Entering is self-cultivation (*sva-pratipatti*);

emerging is transforming others (*para-pariṇāmana*). Thus, the first fifteen and a half chapters represent the Tathāgata’s revelation of the essence, while the subsequent eleven and a half chapters represent the arising [of function].
"Use" (*yòng*) refers to the manifestation of one's own practice (*xing*), while "arising use" (*qǐyòng*) refers to benefiting others;

therefore, the eleven chapters and a half are all of the nature of "arising use" and thus belong to the section on circulation (*liútōng*). Regarding the five chapters from "Bhaiṣajyarāja" (*Yàowáng*) onwards, which concern exhorting others to circulate [the teaching], this refers to:
first, the four bhikṣus; next, Miaozhuāngyán (Subhavyūha); and third, the Lady Jìngdé (Śuddhaguṇā), along with her sons Jìngzàng (Viśuddhanetra) and Jìngyǎn (Viśuddhacakṣus). These are they.

Now, these four—Huade (Flower Virtue), Miaoyin (Wondrous Sound), Yaowang (Medicine King), and Yao Shang (Superior Medicine)—having all together received the wondrous Dharma, have cultivated practice arising from their inherent nature to realize its essence. Now, in order to repay their debt of gratitude, they offer this worship;

thus, after Yaowang comes Miaoyin, within Miaoyin’s section again comes Huade, followed by Tuoluoni (Dhāraṇī), and Yaowang again with Zhunei hu (Protection within Mantras), followed by Yanwang (Adorned King); these four persons are all present therein.

Regarding the question of external protection, since the protection of Samantabhadra has already been established, the first six chapters extensively elaborate upon the "Peaceful Practices" (Anrakugyō).

At the beginning of the circulation of the Honmon (the Original Gate), the initial address to King Bhaiṣajyarāja clarifies the meaning of the first two sections of the circulation of the Kyemotsu-mon (the Gate of Manifested Traces),
specifically the significance of addressing King Bhaiṣajyarāja.
Chapter on the Wondrous Sound: Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara (known as Bodhisattva Siṃhaghoṣa in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*).
First, regarding "Wondrous Sound" (*Gadgada*): it was originally the name of a world-system of worldly music;

second, because he could assist in producing the sound of the wondrous [Dharma], he was named "Wondrous Sound" as a person; third, because he can proclaim the sound of the wondrous Dharma, he is called "Wondrous Sound. This...
Regarding the two meanings: first, it is the sound that proclaims and opens up the *prabheda* (analytical) aspect of the wondrous Dharma, serving as an antidote;

second, it is the sound that proclaims and reveals the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) of the wondrous Dharma. "Analytical" (*prabheda*) refers to the relative, while "revealed" (*prakaṭa*) refers to the absolute.

The initial manifestation of the lotus flower symbolizes the arrival of assistance to inspire the hearing of this wondrous Lotus Sūtra. The presentation of the two questions and answers is precisely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

The *Sūtra* says "listening," and the *Commentary* says "propagating"; these are mentioned alternately. "Listening" refers to one's own practice (*svacaryā*), while "propagating" refers to benefiting others (*parārtha*).

Both listening and propagating belong to the Sublime Sound (*Miaoyin*). In the past, he offered eighty-four thousand bowls made of the seven treasures and attained eighty-four thousand gates of samādhi;
his ability to manifest these eighty-four thousand lotus flowers represents the realization of the causes and effects of the revealed and developed teachings (*kai-xian*) that he heard in the past.
The *Samantabhadra-praśna-samādhi-sūtra* (also known as the *Sūtra on the Samādhi Answered by Samantabhadra*) is a sūtra of response; it contains various jewels within its text.

Regarding the "nineteen expositions of the Dharma," this refers to the manner in which this sūtra is taught according to the text—such as mentioning the east to summon the west—which reveals that the Ten Powers are universally propagated throughout the sūtra.
The Buddha’s response to the inquiries of Śrīguṇarāja and Mañjuśrī concerning the causes and conditions of the activities of Gadgadasvara is precisely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
This reveals and manifests [the truth].
That your body is foremost in its perfect symmetry is precisely the characteristic mark of the *Sudhvaja-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*.

The three bodies of the world are one body; all bodies are the three bodies of the world. Why are they empty? Because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Why do they lack intrinsic nature? Because they arise from causes...

Regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), what constitutes its causal conditions? There are two types of causal conditions: first, false causal conditions; second, true causal conditions.
False conditions consist of ninety-six varieties, which do not exceed eight types of falsity. True conditions refer internally to ignorance as the cause and parents as the condition;
through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, one's own body is produced, which is the "dharma that has arisen. Externally, they refer to various karmic actions.
Taking the four great elements as causes and their conjunction as conditions, the insentient world arises; this refers to the phenomena that are produced.
Since both the sentient and the insentient arise from causes and conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty.
Some say that [the section] following the "Chapter on the Emergence" is the second part, which explains the large numbers and so forth indicated within the initial chapter.
Although the preceding primary outline does not contain this heading, I have provided it here; while the intent is not different, the phrasing is distinct.
However, if one dwells upon the literal meaning, the intent is not met, and the explanation has not yet fully resolved the text. Having no other recourse, I shall attempt [this interpretation].

To explain this: among the two major sections established within the "Longer Period" (jiuzhong), the first fourteen chapters establish the provisional and reveal the real based on the *traces* (*ji*).
From this chapter downward, the [remaining] fourteen chapters establish the provisional and reveal the real based on the *origin* (*ben*).
Now, while we are once again indicating these topical headings, why is it that only this one bears such a name? Is this not a matter of its distinction? One must certainly understand this now.

This means that the term "intention" (*abhiprāya*) is used precisely to clarify the preceding meaning. Why? When we speak of "origin and trace" (*honjaku*), these two both belong to the dependent [the teaching] and do not involve other persons.

Furthermore, when we speak of "opening the provisional to reveal the real" (*kaigen kenshitsu*), this refers specifically to the Trace Gate in terms of the object, and to the Origin Gate in terms of the subject.
As for what they refer to: it refers to those to be converted, namely the three vehicles and the nine realms.
The text states, "All those who seek the three vehicles," and further says, "Desiring to cause all sentient beings [to attain enlightenment]";

this means that for these very people, the teaching is revealed and manifested, as they are all disciples to be transformed, and thus collectively constitute the assembly. The text also states, "The sentient beings therein are all my children.
The meaning of the opening of the Trace Gate lies herein. As for what is called the Fundamental Gate, it refers to the capacity [of the Buddha].
Regarding the "explanation through manifestation," this refers specifically to the Principal of Transformation. The Principal is the Teacher, and the Teacher is the Buddha.

Previously, in relation to those being transformed, there was both the general and the specific: disciples are specific, whereas sentient beings are general. Since the specific requires the general, these two meanings are now presented.
Here, in order to correctly contrast and clarify the previous meaning, it says "Teacher" (which remains general), and thus further cites "Buddha" to provide a precise indication.

That person therefore speaks in terms of both [the provisional and the real]. Regarding the fundamental and the manifested (*honjaku*), when one speaks of "opening the provisional to reveal the real," the manifested is taken as the provisional while the fundamental is the real;

this is because the fundamental has been spontaneously attained since time immemorial, whereas the manifested is the provisional because it is a manifestation shown for the sake of sentient beings during the intervening period from that time until today and into the future. Although the names "provisional" and "real" are the same in these two gates, [their referents differ].
Yet their essential meanings are fundamentally and eternally distinct; to state it briefly, they differ in terms of horizontal and vertical dimensions.
Now, wishing to rely on these few words to clarify the meaning of the two preceding passages, I have adopted this name.

Without these words, the previous passage would state that "the meaning is also difficult to fathom. Nevertheless, both gates should likewise each possess the subjective (the agent) and the objective (the object).

By speaking in terms of specific distinctions, one clarifies the provisional; yet if it were not so, the wondrous intent would be difficult to firmly believe. The author’s achievement is truly marvelous!
However, as the underlying meaning herein is remote and difficult to penetrate in the midst of haste, I shall for now briefly conclude with this.
Trusting that others are capable of proceeding further, I leave it to their reflection.

On the twentieth day of the seventh month of the first year of the Huichang era, the assembly of monks and lay devotees from Wu borrowed this text from the master Shen of Daming Temple in Huating at Lingshi Temple.
This original lacked [certain parts], which were subsequently supplied by Wuchu and others.
This was originally heard in succession; having suddenly suppressed [my thoughts] to examine it thoroughly, I have recorded it.
On the twentieth day of the sixth month of the thirteenth year of Enkyō, the monk Jōman of Senkōin at Enryaku-ji transcribed the Tang edition from the Kai-dan-in.
Thereafter, he [further] transcribed it from the secret manuscript of San’ōin.
Comparing the various editions, the accounts of survival and extinction differ, and the divergent versions are manifold; after a detailed collation from all sides,
it was found that where the records of the retreat differ, and where the texts are inconsistent, even when the *Zhizhiyan* (Eye of Wisdom) examines them again,
the twenty-ninth line at the end of the "Surging Out" chapter appears in some versions placed at the very end, which those who see it will surely understand.
